Installing them all now avoids interruption in the middle of modules. | Pin versions whenever possible and write them down. Terraform, for example, changes behavior between minor versions, and the state is sensitive to this. In pipelines, tools without fixed versions generate builds that break without anyone changing code — one of the most frustrating incidents that exist. | Validation is part of the installation: a command that returns the version and a command that exercises the tool for real. l-1-3.title: Processes, signals, and systemd in practice
l-1-3.objectives: Investigate processes and ports | Send signals correctly | Write a resilient systemd unit
l-1-3.body: Every service is a process with a PID, owner, state, and resources. ps auxf shows the tree, top and htop show live behavior, and ss -tulpn reveals who is listening on which port — a command that solves half of the 'port is in use' issues. States matter: a process in D (uninterruptible I/O) indicates a disk or network problem, not a CPU one; a zombie (Z) indicates a parent that has not reaped its child. | Signals are the civilized way to communicate with processes. SIGTERM (15) requests termination and allows the program to close connections and finalize requests; SIGKILL (9) kills without a chance for cleanup, potentially corrupting state or leaving lock files. Always start with TERM; use KILL as a last resort. | systemd is what ensures the service starts at boot, restarts after failure, and has centralized logs. A well-written unit defines an unprivileged user, working directory, environment variables via EnvironmentFile, restart policy, and basic security limits.
l-1-3.whyItMatters: A service that doesn't restart automatically after a failure turns a two-minute incident into a lost night.
l-1-3.commonMistake: Killing with kill -9 and then discovering corrupted data or a stuck lock file.
l-1-3.productionTip: Use Restart=on-failure with RestartSec to avoid aggressive restart loops, and always test with a reboot.
l-1-3.interviewQuestion: Explain the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL and why it matters in deployment.
l-1-3.glossaryDefs: Definition file for a resource managed by systemd (service, timer, socket). | A process that has terminated but whose status has not yet been collected by its parent process.

l-1-4.title: Logs: finding the root cause with journalctl
l-1-4.objectives: Filter logs by unit, priority, and time | Correlate events between services | Prevent disk full due to logs
l-1-4.body: Logs are the primary source of truth in an incident. With journalctl, you can filter by unit (-u), by priority (-p err), by time window (--since/--until), and follow in real-time (-f). The power lies in combining them: errors from a unit in the last ten minutes, in order, are usually enough to find the first failure — which is often different from the most visible error. | The golden rule is to look for the first error, not the last. Cascading failures hide the origin: a frontend timeout appears after a database connection error. Correlating by timestamp between proxy, application, and database is the skill that separates those who guess from those who diagnose. | Logs are also an operational and security risk: they fill disks and leak sensitive data. Configure rotation and limit the journal, and review what the application writes — tokens, passwords, and personal data should never go into logs.
l-1-4.whyItMatters: Job vacancies ask for troubleshooting. In practice, this means reading logs methodically and proving the cause with evidence.
l-1-4.commonMistake: Restarting the service before collecting logs and losing evidence of what happened.
l-0-5.body: The first task in any new cloud account is not to create a server: it's to reduce risk. Activate MFA on the root account, store root credentials off the work computer, and create a separate user or identity for day-to-day use, with limited permissions. Then set up cost alerts, because almost every student has forgotten to turn off a resource and paid for it. | Configure the AWS CLI with a named profile instead of loose default credentials. Profiles make it explicit which account you are acting on — a simple protection against the classic 'I applied it to the wrong account' mistake. Preferring temporary credentials (SSO/Identity Center) over long-lived keys is the current standard in companies. | Finally, adopt the discipline of destruction: every resource created for study has an expiration date. At the end of each cloud lab, you run the destroy command and verify in the console that nothing is left.
l-0-5.whyItMatters: Cloud job openings require financial responsibility. Knowing how to demonstrate cost control differentiates a junior candidate from a reliable candidate.
l-0-5.commonMistake: Using the root account for everything and leaving NAT Gateway or RDS running after the lab.
l-0-5.productionTip: Tag all resources (project, environment, owner, expiration). Without tags, FinOps does not exist.

l-0-2.title: Professional Linux environment with WSL2 (or VM)
l-0-2.objectives: Install and validate a usable Linux for real work | Configure shell, history, and useful aliases | Understand why working within the Linux filesystem is faster
l-0-2.body: Virtually every server you'll administer runs Linux, so your study environment needs to be Linux. On Windows, the most productive path is WSL2 with Ubuntu LTS: you get a real Linux kernel, integration with VS Code, and Docker without a heavy virtual machine. On macOS, use the native terminal plus a VM or containers to practice systemd. On native Linux, you are already set. | After installing, dedicate fifteen minutes to comfort: a prompt that shows the Git branch, a large history, aliases for repeated commands, and a working directory within the Linux filesystem itself (e.g., ~/projects), never in /mnt/c. Files accessed via /mnt/c go through translation between file systems and make builds and dependency installations drastically slower. | Always validate the environment with commands, not assumptions: distro and version, kernel, available memory, and disk space. This habit is the same one you'll use in the first minute of any incident.
l-0-2.whyItMatters: A fragile environment generates false problems. Half of the 'bugs' for beginners are due to an environment different from the server.
l-0-2.commonMistake: Working in /mnt/c/Users/... and concluding that Docker and npm are slow. The bottleneck is the filesystem bridge.
l-0-2.productionTip: Record the exact version of each installed tool in your journal. Version differences are a common cause of 'it works on my machine'.
l-0-2.interviewQuestion: How do you locally reproduce a problem that only occurs on the server?
l-0-2.glossaryDefs: Windows Subsystem for Linux with a real kernel, allowing Linux distributions to run with good performance. | Long Term Support: a version with extended support, preferred for servers.

l-0-3.title: Git, GitHub, and SSH key: password-less and pain-free access
l-0-3.objectives: Generate and register an ed25519 key | Configure Git identity and default behavior | Create the three project repositories
l-0-3.body: Authenticating via HTTPS with a password or token pasted for each push is unnecessary friction and a risk. An SSH key solves both problems: the private key never leaves your machine, and access can be revoked with one click. Use ed25519, which is short, fast, and the currently recommended standard. | Also configure Git defaults that prevent team confusion: correct name and email, main as the initial branch, pull with rebase to maintain a linear history, and push of the current branch only. These four configurations eliminate a good part of the accidental merges for those learning. | Finally, create the repositories that will support the rest of the course, each with a clear purpose: application, infrastructure, and GitOps manifests. Separating repositories is not being overly fastidious: it's what allows protecting the infrastructure with a different review process than the application.
l-0-3.whyItMatters: Every CI/CD flow starts in a repository. Misconfigured access blocks deployments and becomes a delivery incident.
l-0-3.commonMistake: Pasting the private key instead of the public one on GitHub. If this happens, generate a new pair and revoke the old one.
l-0-3.productionTip: On servers and runners, use deploy keys with read-only permission for only the necessary repository.
l-0-3.securityAlert: Enable 2FA on your GitHub account. A compromised account in an infrastructure repository means access to production.

l-0-1.title: What a DevOps person actually does (and what job openings ask for in 2026)
l-0-1.objectives: Separate myth from real routine in the role | Read a job description and identify what is mandatory and what is desirable | Choose a specialization path consistent with your starting point
l-0-1.body: DevOps is not a magical role between dev and infra: it is the responsibility of shortening the path between a commit and the value delivered in production, with security and reversibility. In practice, your day involves maintaining reliable pipelines, packaging applications, provisioning infrastructure as code, observing behavior in production, responding to incidents, and reducing costs. Those coming from frontend, like you, have a real advantage: they already understand builds, dependencies, environment variables, and what the application needs to run. | Current job openings converge to a very stable core: Linux, networking and HTTP, Git, containers, a cloud provider (AWS leads Portuguese-language job postings), CI/CD (GitHub Actions and GitLab CI dominate), Terraform, Kubernetes, observability (Prometheus/Grafana/OpenTelemetry), and solid notions of security and cost. What changes between announcements is the emphasis: a Platform Engineering opening asks for Kubernetes, Helm, and internal platform experience; an SRE opening asks for SLOs, incidents, and performance; a DevSecOps opening asks for scanners, supply chain, and IAM. | The correct way to study is always the same: you learn a concept, apply it in an artifact of your own project, and write what you learned. On this platform, that artifact is CloudShop — a catalog of 3D products with a Vue frontend, Node API, and PostgreSQL — which you will containerize, publish in a pipeline, provision on AWS via Terraform, migrate to Kubernetes, place under GitOps, and finally instrument with metrics, logs, traces, and SLOs.
l-0-1.whyItMatters: Technical DevOps interviews are conversations about decisions. Those who studied isolated topics answer theory; those who built a project respond with trade-offs, and that's what generates offers.
l-0-1.commonMistake: Starting with Kubernetes without mastering Linux, networking, and containers. The result is copying YAML without understanding why the Pod doesn't start.
l-0-1.productionTip: Keep the technical diary in the repository itself (docs/diario.md). It becomes the basis for the README, the resume, and interview answers.
l-0-1.securityAlert: When creating your cloud account, activate MFA on the root account immediately and never use the root for daily work.
l-0-1.interviewQuestion: Tell me about a production problem you investigated: what signals did you look at first and how did you confirm the root cause?
l-0-1.glossaryDefs: Site Reliability Engineering: applies engineering practices to keep services within measurable targets (SLO). | Building internal platforms and standardized paths for product teams to deliver independently and securely.

l-0-1.codeNote0: Never paste tokens, passwords, or private keys into the diary. Record only the name of the variable used.

l-1-1.objectives: Understand the FHS hierarchy | Quickly find files and content | Inspect large files without freezing the terminal
l-1-1.body: Linux organizes everything in a single tree starting from /. Knowing the meaning of each directory speeds up any investigation: /etc holds configuration, /var variable data (logs, queues, databases), /usr system programs, /opt third-party software, /tmp temporary files, and /proc a live view of the kernel and processes. When someone says 'the config is wrong,' you already know where to look. | Searching is half the battle. find locates by name, size, date, and permission; grep -r locates content; ripgrep does it faster when available. On production servers, combine with head and tail to never open a gigabyte file all at once — a careless cat on a 4 GB log will freeze your session in the middle of a crisis. | Two concepts save time: absolute versus relative paths (in scripts and services, always absolute) and symbolic links, widely used in deployments to point 'current' to the active release and allow for instant rollback.
l-1-1.whyItMatters: In an incident, navigation speed determines how many minutes the service is down. Someone who searches for a file by clicking misses the window.
l-1-1.commonMistake: Using cat on huge files and freezing the SSH session during a crisis.
l-1-1.productionTip: Prefer less +G and tail -f; and always confirm with stat who owns the configuration file.
l-1-1.interviewQuestion: Where would you look for the configuration and logs of an unknown service on a server?
l-1-1.glossaryDefs: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: a convention about the purpose of each directory. | A shortcut that points to another path, used in release/rollback strategies.

l-1-2.title: Permissions, users, and groups without memorization
l-1-2.objectives: Read and write permissions in octal and symbolic | Apply correct ownership to application directories | Use sudo responsibly
l-1-2.body: Permissions in Linux answer three questions: who (owner, group, others), what (read, write, execute), and on what object. In octal, read is 4, write is 2, and execute is 1; therefore 640 means the owner reads and writes, the group reads, others nothing. In directories, execution means 'can enter,' which explains why 644 on a folder breaks access while 755 works. | Most actual deployment failures are due to ownership, not mode: the process runs as user app, but the directory belongs to root. The correct fix is to adjust the owner with chown and grant the minimum necessary — not to hand out 777, which is the equivalent of leaving the door open and writing 'come in'. | Always create a service user without a login shell to run the application. This limits damage in case of compromise and is a requirement for any serious audit.
l-1-2.whyItMatters: Permission errors appear as mysterious deployment failures, uploads that don't save, and services that don't start. Diagnosing them in seconds is a differentiator.
l-1-2.commonMistake: Solving 'permission denied' with chmod -R 777 instead of fixing the owner.
l-1-2.productionTip: Files with credentials: 600 or 640, owned by the service, and never versioned in Git.
l-1-2.securityAlert: Never give sudo without a password to an application user; if it's compromised, the entire server goes down.
l-1-2.interviewQuestion: An upload fails with permission denied. How would you investigate in order?
l-1-2.glossaryDefs: A mask that defines the default permissions for newly created files. | An account without interactive login, created to run services.

l-1-5.title: SSH, Remote Access, and Resource Diagnostics
l-1-5.objectives: Access servers securely and conveniently | Interpret CPU, memory, and disk | Apply basic SSH hardening
l-1-5.body: SSH is the gateway to remote work. Configure ~/.ssh/config with aliases, user, key, and ProxyJump for bastions: besides typing less, you avoid connecting to the wrong host. On the server, minimum hardening is to disable password login and direct root login, allowing only key-based authentication. | When logging into a server with slowness complaints, follow an order: load and CPU (uptime, top), memory and swap (free -h, vmstat), disk space and I/O (df -h, iostat), then network and connections. Load average above the number of cores indicates a queue; active swap indicates memory pressure; high %wa indicates an I/O bottleneck, not processing. | Memory in Linux is confusing: cache is not a leak, it's an optimization. What matters is 'available' and swap activity. And a full disk, often due to logs or container images, produces symptoms that seem like application failures.
l-1-5.whyItMatters: Every infrastructure interview asks the question 'the server is slow, what now?'. Having a roadmap is the answer that gets you approved.
l-1-5.commonMistake: Concluding a memory leak by looking at 'used' without observing 'available' and swap.
l-1-5.productionTip: Monitor inodes in addition to space: millions of small files fill inodes even with 'free' disk space.
l-1-5.securityAlert: Each person should have their own key and user. Shared keys eliminate traceability.

mod-2.title: Networks, HTTP, and Nginx
mod-2.tagline: Follow the packet from the browser to the application process.
mod-2.overview: Almost every production incident is, at its core, a path problem: DNS pointing to the wrong place, blocked port, expired certificate, upstream down. In this module, you'll learn to traverse this path with tools — dig, curl, ss, tcpdump — and operate Nginx as a reverse proxy, truly understanding the difference between 502, 503, and 504.
mod-2.objectives: Explain IP, subnet, gateway, and routes | Diagnose DNS by record, TTL, and queried server | Read HTTP/HTTPS requests with curl and interpret status and headers | Configure Nginx as a reverse proxy with TLS | Differentiate and resolve 502, 503, and 504

Correction: memory limit, automatic restart, and readiness before receiving traffic.

l-2-1.title: IP, Subnets, Ports, and the Packet Path
l-2-1.objectives: Read CIDR addresses and masks | Understand default route and gateway | Identify port blocking
l-2-1.body: An IP address alone means nothing: it needs the mask. 10.0.1.15/24 means the first three octets identify the network and the last one the host, with 254 usable addresses. This concept is the same you'll use when designing VPCs in AWS, where choosing /16 for the VPC and /24 for subnets is the pragmatic standard. | The packet leaves your machine, consults the routing table, finds the default gateway for external destinations, and proceeds. ip route shows this decision; traceroute shows the path. When 'the application is not responding,' the correct question is at which hop the path dies. | Ports identify the service within the host. Connection refused means no one is listening or the firewall actively rejected it; timeout usually means the packet was dropped by a firewall or a wrong route. This distinction saves hours of investigation.
l-2-1.whyItMatters: Without understanding networks, you can't design VPCs, debug Kubernetes, or explain why the internal service is unreachable.
l-2-1.commonMistake: Treating 'connection refused' and 'timeout' as the same problem.
l-2-1.productionTip: Document the IP ranges for each environment before creating the infrastructure; CIDR conflicts are a chronic pain point.
l-2-1.securityAlert: Never expose database ports (5432, 3306) to the internet; use a private network or tunnel.
l-2-1.interviewQuestion: Explain the difference between connection refused and connection timeout.
l-2-1.glossaryDefs: Notation that combines an address and the size of the network prefix, such as 10.0.0.0/16. | Router used for destinations outside the local network.

l-2-4.title: TLS, certificates, and HTTPS that don't expire by surprise
l-2-4.objectives: Understand the TLS handshake | Inspect certificates | Automate renewal
l-2-4.body: In the TLS handshake, the client and server negotiate version and cipher, the server presents the certificate chain, and validation checks signature, name (SAN), and validity. Failing at any of these points produces a browser error and, worse, an error in integrations that don't have someone to click 'proceed'. | Two errors dominate in practice: incomplete chain (works in browser, fails in HTTP client) and expired certificate. Both are detectable by command and both are avoidable by automation with renewal and an alert thirty days before expiration. | On the Nginx side, use TLS 1.2 and 1.3, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, enable HSTS after validating the entire domain, and do not use old protocols. Terminating TLS at the proxy is the standard: the backend receives internal HTTP, and the proxy informs the original scheme via header.
l-2-4.whyItMatters: Expired certificates are one of the most common and most avoidable causes of total unavailability.
l-2-4.commonMistake: Installing only the domain certificate without the intermediate chain.
l-2-4.productionTip: Monitor validity as a metric and alert in 30 days; don't rely only on the renewal cron job.
l-2-4.securityAlert: Disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and weak ciphers; audits will fail, and modern clients no longer need them.
l-2-4.interviewQuestion: A Java client fails on TLS, but the browser works. What is your main hypothesis?
l-2-4.glossaryDefs: Subject Alternative Name: list of domains covered by the certificate. | Header that forces the browser to use HTTPS on the domain for a period.
l-2-4.capstone: Automatically issue and renew the certificate for api.cloudshop.dev.
l-2-4.codeNote0: The certificate's private key must have 600 permissions and root owner. Never version /etc/letsencrypt.
l-2-4.q0: TLS errors only in non-browser clients usually indicate:
l-2-4.q0opts: Expired certificate | Missing intermediate chain | Incorrect DNS | Port 443 closed
l-2-4.q0exp: Browsers complete the chain automatically; strict HTTP clients do not.
l-2-5.title: Nginx reverse proxy and the anatomy of 502, 503, and 504
l-2-5.objectives: Configure reverse proxy with upstream | Adjust timeouts | Diagnose each 5xx by the correct evidence
l-2-5.body: The reverse proxy is the application's front door: it terminates TLS, distributes load, serves static files, applies limits, and hides the internal topology. The minimum configuration defines an upstream, forwards essential headers, and adjusts timeouts consistent with the application's behavior. | The three 5xx errors tell different stories. 502 Bad Gateway: the proxy managed to try, but the upstream refused or closed the connection — typically a crashed process, wrong port, or restart. 503 Service Unavailable: no upstream is available, or the proxy itself is limiting (rate limit, all backends marked as failed). 504 Gateway Timeout: the upstream accepted but took longer than proxy_read_timeout — almost always a slow query or a stuck dependency. | The procedure is always the same: read the Nginx error.log (the message in parentheses is gold), test the upstream directly with curl, check who is listening on the port, and only then change configuration. Increasing the timeout without understanding the cause turns a fast error into prolonged slowness.
l-2-1.q0exp: 256 total addresses minus network and broadcast result in 254 usable ones.
l-2-2.title: DNS: records, TTL, and why the change didn't propagate
l-2-2.objectives: Query records with dig | Choose between A, CNAME, and ALIAS | Plan IP change with low TTL
l-2-2.body: DNS translates names to addresses, and each record type plays a role: A points to IPv4, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME to another name, MX for email, TXT for verifications and SPF, NS delegates the zone. In AWS, the ALIAS record resolves the CNAME limitation on the root domain by pointing directly to an ALB or CloudFront. | TTL is the cache duration. If you are going to switch servers, reduce the TTL to 60 seconds a few hours before; otherwise, some users will continue to go to the old IP for hours. That's why 'I already changed the DNS and it still doesn't work' is almost always cache, not an error. | When diagnosing, consult the authoritative server and not just the local resolver: dig +trace shows the complete chain, and comparing your resolver's response with the authoritative one immediately reveals if the problem is propagation.
l-2-2.whyItMatters: Infrastructure migration without a DNS plan generates partial and hard-to-explain unavailability.
l-2-2.commonMistake: Changing the record with a 24h TTL and promising the change will be immediate.
l-2-2.productionTip: Before any migration, lower the TTL, validate the new destination, migrate, and only then return the TTL to a high value.
l-2-2.interviewQuestion: Why isn't CNAME used in the root domain and what is the alternative in AWS?
l-2-2.glossaryDefs: Time in seconds that a record can be cached. | Server that officially holds the zone's records.
l-2-2.capstone: Create api.cloudshop.dev with TTL 60 during the migration phase.
l-2-2.q0: You changed the A record but some users still go to the old IP. Most likely cause?
l-2-2.q0opts: Firewall blocking | DNS cache by TTL | Invalid certificate | Wrong MX record
l-2-2.q0exp: Resolvers keep the previous response cached until the TTL expires.
l-2-3.title: HTTP, status, and headers with curl
l-2-3.objectives: Interpret status families | Use curl to truly debug | Understand headers that affect proxy and cache
l-2-3.body: HTTP status is the first piece of information for any diagnosis: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx caller error, 5xx server error. Naive reading confuses 401 (unauthenticated) with 403 (authenticated, but unauthorized) and 404 (not found) with 400 (malformed request) — distinctions that define whether the problem is client-side or server-side. | curl is the Swiss Army knife: -I shows only headers, -v reveals handshake and redirects, -w extracts times per phase (DNS, connection, TLS, first byte). Measuring time per phase transforms 'it's slow' into 'the TLS handshake takes 800 ms', which is a statement that can be fixed. | Headers matter in operation: Host defines the virtual host, X-Forwarded-For carries the client's real IP behind the proxy, Cache-Control decides CDN behavior, and Content-Type prevents misinterpreted responses. A misconfigured proxy that loses these headers generates hard-to-reproduce bugs.
l-2-3.whyItMatters: curl is the tool that proves where the problem lies before blaming another team.
l-2-3.commonMistake: Testing in the browser with cache and extensions and drawing incorrect conclusions about the API.
l-2-3.productionTip: Every service should have a simple /health (without dependencies) and /ready (with dependencies) for proxy and Kubernetes use.
l-2-3.interviewQuestion: Differentiate 401, 403, and 404 and explain what each indicates in an investigation.
l-2-3.glossaryDefs: Time To First Byte: time until the first byte of response, useful for separating network from processing. | Header that preserves the client's original IP behind proxies.
l-3-1.body: For most teams, trunk-based development with short-lived branches outperforms complex workflows: you create feat/something, deliver it in less than two days, open a PR, CI validates it, and the merge happens. Long-lived branches accumulate conflicts and turn integration into a traumatic event. | Commits are documentation. Conventional Commits (feat, fix, chore, docs, refactor) allow for automatic changelog generation and tell the reader the intent of the change. A good commit answers what changed and why; the how is in the diff. | Protecting main is an engineering decision, not bureaucracy: requiring PRs, reviews, and checks prevents untested code from reaching production. It's also the point where CI/CD begins to provide real value.
l-3-1.whyItMatters: Pipelines, GitOps, and rollbacks depend on a predictable history. A chaotic repository contaminates all automation.
l-3-1.commonMistake: Committing everything in a single giant commit with the message 'adjustments'.
l-3-1.productionTip: Squash merge keeps main clean and facilitates reverting an entire change.
l-3-1.securityAlert: Enable secret scanning in the repository; a committed token must be revoked, not just removed.
l-3-1.interviewQuestion: How would you organize the branch workflow for a team of five people?
l-3-1.glossaryDefs: A strategy with short-lived branches integrated frequently into main. | A merge that condenses all commits of a PR into a single commit.

l-3-1.q0exp: The smaller the divergence between the branch and main, the lower the chance of conflict.
l-3-2.title: Merge, rebase, revert: rewriting or preserving history
l-3-2.objectives: Resolve conflicts safely | Apply rebase only where it is safe | Revert published changes
l-3-2.body: Merge preserves history as it happened and creates a merge commit; rebase reapplies your commits on top of the current base, producing a straight line. The practical rule is simple: rebase on your local branch before a PR, merge to integrate into main. Rebasing on a shared branch rewrites commits that others already have and creates real confusion. | Conflict is not an error: it's Git telling you that two changes touched the same section, and it can't decide. You open the file, choose the correct result (which sometimes is neither side), mark it as resolved, and continue. Testing after resolving is mandatory: a poorly resolved conflict might compile but still break the logic. | To undo something already published, use revert: it creates a new commit reversing the change and keeps the history auditable. reset --hard on a shared branch is the fastest way to lose colleagues' work.
l-3-2.whyItMatters: Fast rollbacks depend on reliable history. Revert is the deploy emergency button.
l-3-2.commonMistake: Rebasing a branch that already has an open PR and force pushing, invalidating reviews.
l-3-2.productionTip: If a deploy broke production, revert first and investigate later. Restoring service comes before understanding.
l-3-2.interviewQuestion: Explain when revert is preferable to reset and why.
l-3-2.glossaryDefs: Local record of all HEAD positions, allowing 'lost' commits to be recovered. | A forced push that fails if the remote has commits you haven't seen.
l-3-2.capstone: Revert a configuration change that broke the CloudShop build.
l-3-2.codeNote0: Never use push --force on a shared branch; if necessary, use --force-with-lease.
l-3-2.q0: Which command undoes an already published commit without rewriting history?
l-3-2.q0opts: git reset --hard | git revert | git rebase -i | git checkout
l-3-2.q0exp: revert creates a reverse commit, preserving the shared history.
l-3-3.title: Tags, releases, and semantic versioning
l-3-3.objectives: Apply SemVer | Create annotated tags and releases | Relate tag, image, and deploy
l-3-3.body: Versioning is not just for show: it's what allows you to say exactly what is in production and revert to a known point. SemVer uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where MAJOR indicates a breaking change, MINOR a compatible new feature, and PATCH a bug fix. | Annotated tags store author, date, and message, and are the natural trigger for release pipelines. From the tag, you build the image with the same identifier, so that the code version and the artifact version never diverge. | Avoid the latest tag as a production reference: it changes underneath you and destroys reproducibility. Production always points to an immutable version.
l-3-3.whyItMatters: Without an immutable version, there's no reliable rollback or audit of what's running.
l-3-3.commonMistake: Only using latest and then not being able to reproduce what was in production yesterday.
l-3-3.productionTip: Reference the image by digest (sha256) in critical environments: it's the maximum guarantee of immutability.
l-3-3.interviewQuestion: How do you ensure that the version in production exactly corresponds to a commit?
l-3-3.glossaryDefs: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH versioning convention with defined meaning. | sha256 hash that immutably identifies an image's content.

l-3-4.title: Serious Bash: set -euo pipefail, functions, and exit codes
l-3-4.objectives: Write scripts that fail early and loud | Use functions, trap, and logging | Return useful exit codes
l-3-4.body: An automation script without error handling is a trap: it continues after failing and produces a worse state than the initial one. set -e aborts on error, set -u fails on an undefined variable (avoiding rm -rf on an empty path), set -o pipefail propagates errors in a pipeline, and an adjusted IFS prevents breakage with spaces in names. | Exit code is your script's interface to the world: 0 is success and any other value is failure. CI, systemd, cron, and Kubernetes make decisions based on this. Defining specific codes (2 for missing dependency, 3 for failed validation) makes automation readable. | Structure with small functions, log with timestamp to stderr, use trap for temporary file cleanup, and validate arguments at the beginning. And run ShellCheck: it finds quoting bugs in seconds that would cost hours.
l-3-4.whyItMatters: Bash appears in every job because it's the glue for any automation: pipelines, entrypoints, and on-call routines.
l-3-4.commonMistake: Forgetting quotes around a variable with a space and deleting the wrong file.
l-3-4.productionTip: Add shellcheck to CI. It's the cheapest and most profitable linter available.
l-3-4.interviewQuestion: What does each part of set -euo pipefail do and what problem does it prevent?
l-3-4.glossaryDefs: Registers a command to execute when the script receives a signal or terminates. | Number returned by the process; 0 indicates success.
l-3-4.capstone: Use the health-check in the host's cron and as a post-deploy verification command.
l-3-4.codeNote0: Always use quotes for variables and never build commands by concatenating external input: it's a shell injection risk.
l-3-4.q0: Which option makes the script abort when a command within a pipeline fails?
l-3-4.q0exp: Without pipefail, the pipeline status is only based on the last command.
l-3-5.title: Automate on-call tasks: log backup and cron/timers
l-3-5.objectives: Write backup with retention | Schedule with cron and systemd timer | Validate restoration
l-3-5.body: Repetitive on-call tasks are prime candidates for automation: compressing logs, cleaning old files, checking disk space, checking certificates. The script needs to be idempotent (running it twice causes no harm) and observable (log and exit code). | A backup without a restoration test is an illusion of security. Always validate the integrity of the generated file and, periodically, restore it to another path to verify. Retention needs to be explicit: how many days, where, who pays for storage. | For scheduling, cron remains ubiquitous, but systemd timers offer integrated logging with journal, dependencies, and Persistent=true to execute after a reboot. On modern servers, timers are the better choice; in legacy environments, cron works.
l-3-5.whyItMatters: Automating repetitive tasks frees up engineering time and reduces human error during late-night on-call shifts.
l-3-5.commonMistake: Backup that has been running for months on a path that changed — and no one checked.
l-3-5.productionTip: Have the script emit a metric or success notification; silence is not evidence of proper functioning.
l-3-5.securityAlert: Cron running as root with a script writable by another user is a privilege escalation vulnerability.
l-3-5.interviewQuestion: What is the advantage of systemd timer over cron on a modern server?
l-3-5.glossaryDefs: An operation whose result is the same when executed more than once. | A timer option that executes the missed task after the host restarts.

l-3-5.q0opts: See the file size | List the tar content and test restoration | Trust the tar exit code | Count the source files

mod-4.overview: Container is the modern unit of delivery. Here you will learn to build small and secure images, understand layer caching, manage data with volumes, connect services in networks, and orchestrate the complete CloudShop stack — Vue frontend, Node API, and PostgreSQL — with Docker Compose, including health checks and environment variables.

l-4-1.title: Images, containers, and the correct mental model
l-4-1.objectives: Distinguish image, container, and registry | Operate the container lifecycle | Inspect what is running
l-4-1.body: An image is a read-only template, formed by stacked layers; a container is a running instance of that template, with its own ephemeral write layer. A registry is where images are stored (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR). Understanding this explains why data written inside the container disappears when you recreate it — and why volumes exist. | A container is not a virtual machine: it shares the host's kernel and isolates processes using namespaces and cgroups. This makes it lightweight and fast, but also means it's not a perfect security boundary — hence the importance of not running as root and limiting resources. | The container lives as long as its main process (PID 1) lives. If the process terminates, the container stops. This is why so many containers 'fail to start': the command finished, successfully or with an error, and Docker simply obeyed.
l-4-1.whyItMatters: Everything else (CI/CD, Kubernetes, GitOps) assumes you understand containers. A wrong mental model here contaminates everything.
l-4-1.commonMistake: Storing important data in the container's write layer and losing it on the next deploy.
l-4-1.productionTip: Treat containers as disposable: nothing essential inside, everything in a volume or external service.
l-4-1.interviewQuestion: Why does a container stop immediately after starting?
l-4-1.glossaryDefs: Immutable image layer, reused in cache and across images. | Kernel mechanism that limits CPU, memory, and I/O for a group of processes.

l-4-1.q0: What happens to data written inside the container when it is removed?
l-4-1.q0opts: They remain on the host | They are lost, unless they are in a volume | They go to the image | They go to the registry
l-4-1.q0exp: The write layer is discarded with the container; persistence requires a volume or bind mount.

l-5-1.title: Anatomy of a workflow: triggers, jobs, and steps
l-5-1.objectives: Choose appropriate triggers | Structure parallel and dependent jobs | Use a version matrix
l-5-1.body: A workflow reacts to events: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch (manual), and release. The choice of trigger defines the cost and utility: validating on pull_request protects main; publishing on tag push ensures that only tagged versions generate artifacts. | Jobs run in parallel by default and on separate machines, which means nothing is automatically shared between them — use needs to order and artifacts to transport files. Steps within a job share the same runner and directory. | Matrix is the way to test multiple versions without duplicating YAML, and concurrency cancels old executions of the same branch, saving minutes and avoiding result confusion.

l-4-4.title: Docker Compose: the CloudShop stack in one command
l-4-4.objectives: Declare multiple services | Use healthcheck and conditional depends_on | Separate configuration by environment
l-4-4.body: Compose describes the entire environment in YAML: services, networks, volumes, and dependencies. The real gain is not typing less, it's reproducibility: anyone can clone the repository, run one command, and have the same environment — goodbye two-day onboarding. | depends_on alone only orders startup; it does not wait for the service to be ready. For that, there is healthcheck combined with condition: service_healthy. Without this, the API starts before PostgreSQL accepts connections and enters a restart loop — the most common error for beginners. | Separate what changes per environment: a base docker-compose.yml and an override for development with bind mount and hot reload. In production, you don't use Compose with bind mount for code; you use the image built in the pipeline.
l-4-4.whyItMatters: Compose is the standard development environment for teams that deliver containers — and the natural step up to Kubernetes.
l-4-4.commonMistake: Relying on depends_on without healthcheck and blaming the application for the CrashLoop.
l-4-4.productionTip: Run docker compose config in CI to detect invalid YAML before merging.

l-4-5.title: Multi-stage and image security
l-4-5.objectives: Separate build from runtime | Run as a non-root user with read-only filesystem | Scan for vulnerabilities
l-4-5.body: Multi-stage build resolves an old conflict: to compile you need a compiler, dev dependencies, and tools; to run, you only need the artifact. With separate stages, the final result contains only what is necessary — smaller image, faster build, and reduced attack surface. | Container security has a short and mandatory list: non-root user, no embedded secrets, updated and pinned base image, read-only filesystem where possible, discarded capabilities, and defined resource limits. Each of these items appears in a real audit checklist. | Image scanning in the pipeline turns security into a process. Fail the build on critical vulnerabilities with available fixes and generate SBOM to know what's inside the artifact — a growing requirement in corporate contracts.
l-4-5.whyItMatters: Large images cost pipeline time and registry money; insecure images cost incidents.
l-4-2.body: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer, and Docker reuses the layer if the input hasn't changed. Hence the golden rule: first copy dependency files (package.json and lock), install, and only then copy the code. Inverting this order, any single line code change invalidates the installation and the build takes minutes again. | .dockerignore is as important as the Dockerfile: without it, local node_modules, .git, and .env files go into the build context, making everything slow and potentially leaking secrets into the image. | Base image choice defines size and attack surface. Alpine is tiny but uses musl (which sometimes breaks native binaries); Debian slim variants are a good middle ground; distroless delivers the minimum to run, without a shell — excellent for production.
l-4-2.whyItMatters: An 8-minute build turns into 40 seconds with correct ordering — a direct impact on the team's delivery time.
l-4-2.commonMistake: COPY . . before npm ci, destroying the cache on every code change.

l-4-3.title: Volumes, networks, and environment variables
l-4-3.objectives: Persist data correctly | Connect containers via network and internal DNS | Inject configuration without recompiling
l-4-3.body: Named volumes are the correct way to persist database data: managed by Docker, portable, and with adequate performance. Bind mounts point to a host directory and are ideal for development to see code changes instantly — but they expose host paths and, in production, create undesirable coupling. | Every network created by Docker includes internal DNS: containers find each other by service name. This is why the API accesses the database at db:5432, not localhost. Keeping the database on an internal network, without publishing a port to the host, is elemental good security practice. | Configuration comes from the environment, not from the code. Publish variables for host, port, and database name; for credentials, use orchestrator secrets or a mounted file with restricted permissions. The same artifact needs to run in dev, staging, and production by simply changing the environment.
l-4-3.whyItMatters: Losing the database volume in a deploy is the kind of error that costs jobs. Understanding persistence is mandatory.
l-4-3.commonMistake: Using localhost to talk to another container and getting ECONNREFUSED.

l-5-3.objectives: Manage secrets by environment | Authenticate to AWS without static keys | Apply least privilege to the workflow token
l-5-3.body: Secrets in CI are targets for attacks. Best practices: use secrets per environment with an approval rule, never print values, avoid passing secrets via command-line arguments, and restrict who can trigger workflows that access production. | The most important evolution in recent years is OIDC: instead of storing an AWS access key in GitHub, the workflow exchanges an identity token for temporary credentials by assuming a role. There's no key to leak or rotate, and the role precisely limits what the pipeline can do, including per repository and branch. | Add to this the minimum permissions for GITHUB_TOKEN (contents: read by default, write only where necessary) and you eliminate most pipeline compromise vectors.
l-5-3.whyItMatters: Higher-level job openings explicitly ask about OIDC and least privilege in CI.
l-5-3.commonMistake: Storing AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in the repository and never rotating it.
l-5-3.productionTip: Use protected environments with mandatory reviewers for production deployments.

Publishing to GHCR with docker/build-push-action and docker/metadata-action automatically generates consistent tags: the Git tag version, the commit SHA, and optionally, 'latest' for development convenience — never for production. | The digest is the image's true identity. Record it in the job output and use it for deployment: this ensures the same tested image is the one running, with no chance of someone overwriting a tag along the way. | Add OCI labels (source, revision, version) so anyone can trace the image back to the commit. In an audit and during an incident, this detail saves a lot of time.
l-5-4.whyItMatters: Deploying by digest guarantees that production runs exactly what passed the tests.
l-5-4.commonMistake: Deploying :latest and not being able to tell which commit is running.

l-5-5.title: Deploy, rollback, and debugging a broken pipeline
l-5-5.objectives: Structure deploy with approval | Perform rollback in minutes | Debug workflow with a method
l-5-5.body: Deploy without a planned rollback is a gamble. The minimum standard is: an immutable artifact, a known previous version, and a tested path back — whether it's a manual job that redeploys the previous version or a rollout undo in Kubernetes. Rollback needs to be so routine that no one hesitates to use it at three in the morning. | To debug a pipeline, follow this order: read the first error in the log (not the last), reproduce the command locally with the same versions, check environment differences (variables, permissions, cache), and only then modify the YAML. Activate detailed debug when necessary and use act to iterate locally without cluttering the execution history. | Three causes cover most cases: missing variable or secret in the context (fork PRs do not receive secrets), insufficient token permissions, and version difference between the local machine and the runner.
l-5-5.whyItMatters: DORA metrics value restore time. Fast rollback is the practical answer.
l-5-5.commonMistake: Trying to fix forward under pressure instead of reverting and investigating calmly.
l-5-5.productionTip: Post-deploy health check with automatic rollback on failure is the standard that prevents late nights.
l-5-5.securityAlert: Fork PRs do not receive secrets: pipelines that depend on them fail and attempt insecure workarounds.
l-5-5.interviewQuestion: Describe your process for debugging a workflow that only fails on the runner.

l-6-1.title: IAM: identities, roles, and least privilege
l-6-1.objectives: Distinguish user, role, and policy | Write a minimal policy | Eliminate static keys
l-6-1.body: IAM is the most important AWS service because mistakes are expensive: a permissive policy turns a bug into a security incident. A user represents a person, a role is an identity assumable by a service or federation, and a policy is the JSON document that authorizes actions on resources, with conditions. | Least privilege is a process, not a state: start restricted, collect actual denials, and only grant what's necessary. Tools like Access Analyzer and CloudTrail logs show which permissions were effectively used — an objective basis for reducing scope. | The most valuable practical rule: an application on EC2, Lambda, or ECS uses a role attached to the instance/task, and a pipeline uses OIDC. Long-term access keys only when there's no alternative, with mandatory rotation and never in a repository.
l-6-1.whyItMatters: Every audit and every cloud incident goes through IAM. Explaining least privilege with an example is a differentiator in an interview.
l-6-1.commonMistake: Attaching AdministratorAccess to the application's role 'to unblock it' and never reviewing it again.
l-6-1.productionTip: Use tags on roles and tag-based policies: scales better than per-resource policies.
l-6-1.securityAlert: IAM keys in a public repository are exploited in minutes by bots. Revoke and audit CloudTrail immediately.
l-6-1.interviewQuestion: How would you grant access to a specific bucket for an application without using keys?

l-6-2.title: VPC, subnets, routes, IGW, and NAT
l-6-2.objectives: Design VPC with tiers | Understand what makes a subnet public | Decide on NAT considering cost
l-6-2.body: Your VPC is your isolated network in the cloud. The standard production design has three tiers: public subnets (ALB and NAT), private application subnets, and private data subnets. Distribute them across at least two Availability Zones — a requirement for Multi-AZ RDS and for fault tolerance. | What makes a subnet 'public' is not its name: it's the route table pointing 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway. A private subnet uses a NAT Gateway to go out (update packages, call APIs) without accepting inbound connections. Confusing this is the classic origin of databases exposed to the internet. | Pay attention to costs: NAT Gateway is billed per hour and per data processed, being one of the biggest bill villains in a learning environment. Alternatives: VPC endpoints for S3/ECR, a small NAT instance in a lab, or simply destroy the environment at the end of the day.
l-6-2.whyItMatters: Without understanding routes and subnets, you won't debug 'the application cannot reach the database' nor design an auditable environment.
l-6-2.commonMistake: Placing RDS in a public subnet to 'facilitate access' and exposing the database.
l-6-2.productionTip: Reserve ranges per environment (dev 10.20/16, staging 10.30/16, prod 10.40/16) to allow future peering without conflict.
l-6-2.securityAlert: Unrestricted outbound flow is also a risk: data exfiltration happens via 443. Consider VPC endpoints.
l-6-2.interviewQuestion: What exactly differentiates a public subnet from a private one?
l-6-2.glossaryDefs: Internet Gateway: a component that allows traffic between the VPC and the internet. | A service that allows private subnets to go out to the internet, without inbound access.

l-6-2.q0exp: The route table with a destination to the IGW defines the subnet as public.
l-6-3.title: Security Groups, NACLs, and Minimum Exposure
l-6-3.objectives: Configure SG with inter-group referencing | Distinguish SG from NACL | Audit account exposure
l-6-3.body: A Security Group is a stateful firewall, applied to the network interface: you declare what comes in, and the response goes out automatically. An NACL is stateless, applied to the subnet, and requires both inbound and outbound rules — used as a coarse additional layer, not as the primary control. | The technique that separates amateur from professional is to reference SGs instead of CIDRs: the database's SG allows 5432 only from the application's SG. This way, when new instances come online, the permission automatically follows, and no IP needs to be manually maintained. | Auditing exposure should be a weekly routine: look for rules with 0.0.0.0/0 on administrative or database ports. Finding 22 or 5432 open to the world is the most common — and most exploited — discovery.
l-6-3.whyItMatters: This is literally the boss of the module and one of the most common findings in a real audit.
l-6-3.commonMistake: Temporarily opening 0.0.0.0/0 to test and forgetting to close it.
l-6-3.productionTip: Prefer SSM Session Manager over SSH: audited access, no open port, and no key to leak.
l-6-3.securityAlert: A database accessible via the internet with a weak password is compromised in hours by automated scanning.

l-6-5.body: Cloud cost is an engineering responsibility. The champions of unexpected bills are NAT Gateway, idle Elastic IPs, orphaned EBS volumes, old snapshots, forgotten load balancers, and egress traffic. Knowing this list already prevents most surprises. | Without tags, there is no analysis: project, environment, owner, and validity allow attributing expenses and hunting down orphaned resources. Then come budgets with percentage-based alerts and anomaly detection for sudden variations. | Adopt the discipline of destruction: every lab ends with destroy and an active verification of remaining resources. In Terraform, this is a command; without IaC, it's a manual checklist—one more argument in favor of describing everything in code.
l-6-5.whyItMatters: Current job openings explicitly mention FinOps. Being able to discuss costs with numbers differentiates candidates.
l-6-5.commonMistake: Leaving a NAT Gateway on for an entire month for a two-hour lab.
l-6-5.productionTip: Automate nightly shutdown of development environments; 60% savings are common.
l-6-5.securityAlert: Unexplained cost spikes can be a sign of a compromised account used for mining. Investigate as an incident.
l-6-5.interviewQuestion: Which resources would you check first if the bill doubled without a new deploy?
l-6-5.glossaryDefs: A practice of financial management of the cloud, uniting engineering and finance. | A resource that continues to incur charges without being associated with anything in use.

With Terraform, you declare the infrastructure, version it in Git, and apply it with review; with Ansible, you configure what runs inside hosts idempotently. Here, you'll provision identical dev and staging environments, learn remote state with lock, reusable modules, and how to identify and resolve drift—the difference between code and reality.

l-7-3.title: Modules, reuse, and combating drift
l-7-3.objectives: Write module with clear interface | Reuse across environments | Automatically detect drift
l-7-3.body: A module is the unit of reuse: inputs (variables), logic (resources), and outputs. A good module has a small interface, sensible default values, and no hidden assumptions about the environment. Network, application, and database modules cover most of the needs of a project the size of CloudShop. | Drift is the divergence between the code and reality, usually caused by manual changes in the console during an emergency. The problem is not just aesthetic: the next apply could undo an urgent fix or destroy something that has become necessary. | The defense is a process: a scheduled plan in CI that fails when there's a difference, notification to the team, and a clear rule that manual changes must be reflected in the code on the same day. When a resource already exists outside Terraform, use import (or import blocks) to bring it under control.
l-7-3.whyItMatters: Drift is the boss of this territory and a real pain point for every team that operates cloud at scale.
l-7-3.commonMistake: Creating a giant module with dozens of variables that no one understands or reuses.

l-7-4.title: Ansible: inventory, playbooks, and idempotence
l-7-4.objectives: Write inventory and playbook | Ensure idempotence | Use handlers and variables
l-7-4.body: Terraform creates the infrastructure; Ansible configures what runs inside it. It acts via SSH, without an agent, and is declarative by module: you say 'the package should be present' and 'the service should be running' — you don't write the commands. This is what produces idempotence. | Idempotence is the heart of Ansible: applying the playbook twice should result in changed=0 on the second run. When you resort to the shell/command module without creates or changed_when, you lose this guarantee and return to the world of unpredictable scripts. | Organize with roles when the playbook grows: separate tasks, handlers, templates, defaults, and vars. Jinja2 templates generate configuration per environment, and handlers restart services only when the configuration has actually changed.
l-7-4.whyItMatters: Many companies still operate fleets of VMs; Ansible is the standard for configuring them with predictability.
l-7-1.objectives: Write provider, resource, variable, and output | Understand init/plan/apply/destroy | Comprehend what the state stores
l-7-1.body: Terraform is declarative: you describe the desired state and it calculates the change plan. The cycle is init (downloads providers and configures backend), plan (shows the diff), apply (executes), and destroy (removes). Reading the plan before applying is a professional obligation, not a formality. | The state is the map between the code and the real resources, including attributes and dependencies. Losing the state means Terraform no longer knows what it manages; corrupting it through two simultaneous executions means duplicated or destroyed resources. Therefore: remote backend, versioning, and lock. | Security alert: the state contains sensitive values in plain text (generated passwords, endpoints, keys). It never goes into Git; it goes into a private, encrypted bucket with restricted access.
l-7-1.whyItMatters: IaC is an almost universal requirement in job postings; explaining state and plan is a recurring interview question.
l-7-1.commonMistake: Running apply without reading the plan and destroying a resource with data.
l-7-1.productionTip: Save the plan to a file and apply exactly that plan: it avoids surprises between review and apply.
l-7-1.securityAlert: State in a public bucket is a credential and topology leak. Block public access and enable encryption.
l-7-1.interviewQuestion: What happens if two engineers run apply at the same time without a lock?
l-7-1.glossaryDefs: Plugin that translates Terraform configuration into API calls of a platform. | File that maps declared resources to real resources and their attributes.

l-7-2.title: Remote backend, lock, and environment separation
l-7-2.objectives: Configure S3 backend with lock | Securely separate environments | Protect the state
l-7-2.body: As soon as a second person touches the infrastructure, the state needs to leave your machine. The standard on AWS is an S3 bucket with versioning and encryption, plus a lock (DynamoDB in classic versions, or S3 lockfile in more recent ones). A lock prevents concurrent executions, and versioning allows recovery of a corrupted state. | For environments, two paths: workspaces (simpler, same backend, different keys) or directories per environment with their own tfvars (more explicit and more common in production, because it allows different permissions per account and prevents accidental apply in the wrong environment). | Regardless of the choice, automatically run plan on every infrastructure PR and require approval for apply in production. Infrastructure deserves the same rigor of review as application code — in practice, even more.
l-7-2.whyItMatters: Shared state without a lock is the proven recipe for corrupted infrastructure in a team.
l-7-2.commonMistake: Committing terraform.tfstate to Git — and with it, internal passwords and endpoints.
l-7-2.productionTip: Separate AWS accounts per environment provide the strongest isolation; within the same account, use distinct roles per environment.
l-7-2.securityAlert: force-unlock without confirming that no one else is applying can permanently corrupt the state.
l-7-2.interviewQuestion: How would you organize Terraform for three environments with different teams?
l-7-2.glossaryDefs: Where Terraform stores the state and coordinates the lock. | Separate instances of state within the same configuration.

l-7-4.productionTip: Always run with --check --diff before applying to production and keep ansible-lint in CI.
l-7-4.securityAlert: Playbook with become and shell module receiving an external variable is an arbitrary execution vector.

l-7-5.body: The mature flow is: Terraform provisions and exposes outputs (IPs, IDs, endpoints), a dynamic inventory consumes this data, and Ansible configures the hosts. No manual IP copying — coupling by output is what makes the process repeatable. | In the pipeline, clearly separate plan (in PR, with read-only role, result commented in PR) from apply (in main or tag, with protected environment and human approval). This separation allows infrastructure to be reviewed like code. | Record in the repository the execution order, prerequisites, and the infrastructure rollback procedure — which is rarely 'destroy'. For resources with data, rollback means restoring a backup, not deleting and recreating.
l-7-5.whyItMatters: Provisioning and configuring in a single, auditable flow is exactly what the job description calls infrastructure automation.
l-7-5.commonMistake: Applying Terraform from the local machine and then not knowing who changed what.
l-7-5.productionTip: Automatically comment the plan in the PR: infrastructure review becomes accessible to the whole team.
l-7-5.securityAlert: Never grant apply permission to a workflow triggered by a PR from a fork.

l-8-2.title: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and Secret

l-8-2.body: Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which manage pods, and it's what allows gradual rollout and rollback. Service provides a stable name and load balancing for a set of pods selected by labels: ClusterIP for internal use, NodePort for direct access in a lab environment, LoadBalancer to provision a load balancer in the cloud. | Configuration comes from ConfigMap; sensitive data comes from Secret. Important: Standard Secret is just base64, not encryption — what protects it is RBAC, encryption at rest in etcd, and not versioning the value. For GitOps, use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or External Secrets Operator. | Labels and selectors are the glue for everything. A Service selector that doesn't match the pod labels results in the classic 'Service without endpoints,' where the application is running but nothing reaches it.
l-8-2.whyItMatters: These four objects cover 80% of daily work with Kubernetes.

Without a controller installed, the Ingress object exists, and nothing happens — a frequent confusion for beginners. | With Ingress, you centralize host and path routing, TLS, and policies like redirects and rate limits at a single entry point. In CloudShop, the frontend responds at the root and the API at /api, with the same certificate. | cert-manager automates certificate issuance and renewal via ACME, transforming a recurring risk (expired certificate) into a process. In production, also monitor validity as a metric.
l-8-3.whyItMatters: Every application needs to be reachable via HTTPS; Ingress is the standard mechanism for this.
l-8-3.commonMistake: Creating Ingress without a controller installed and concluding that 'Kubernetes doesn't work'.
l-8-3.productionTip: Ingress timeouts should be consistent with application timeouts, as in traditional Nginx.

l-8-1.title: Cluster Architecture and the Reconciliation Loop
l-8-1.objectives: Understand control plane and nodes | Create a local cluster | Navigate resources with kubectl
l-8-1.body: Kubernetes works by reconciliation: you declare the desired state in the API server, etcd stores it, and controllers compare it with the actual state and act until convergence. Understanding this explains why deleting a pod manually makes it reappear — the Deployment wants three replicas and the controller obeys this desire, not yours. | The control plane includes the API server, etcd, scheduler, and controller manager; on each node, kubelet (executes and reports), container runtime, and kube-proxy (service networking). Diagnosis always starts with events and status, which reflect what the controllers observed. | Kind creates a complete cluster in Docker containers, ideal for learning and for CI. Start by mastering kubectl get/describe/logs/exec and the use of namespaces — most of the daily work is in these five commands.
l-8-1.whyItMatters: Without the reconciliation model in mind, you will fight the cluster instead of operating it.

l-8-4.title: Probes, resources, autoscaling, and RBAC
l-8-4.objectives: Configure probes that help instead of hinder | Define requests/limits with criteria | Apply HPA and minimal RBAC
l-8-4.body: Liveness says 'if it fails, restart'; readiness says 'if it fails, don't send traffic'; startup gives extra time for slow-starting applications. The classic mistake is to point liveness to an endpoint that checks the database: when the database fluctuates, Kubernetes restarts the entire application and turns a degradation into a total outage. | Requests define what the scheduler reserves; limits, the ceiling. CPU above the limit suffers throttling (becomes slow); memory above the limit results in OOMKilled (the container dies). Defining memory with real leeway and observing consumption before tightening is the correct practice. | HPA scales replicas by metric, but only works with defined requests and an active metrics-server. And RBAC closes the loop: each application and each person with the minimum necessary, never cluster-admin distributed for convenience.
l-8-4.whyItMatters: Poorly implemented probes and limits are the number one cause of instability in real-world clusters.
l-8-4.commonMistake: Liveness pointing to an endpoint that depends on the database, causing cascading restarts.
l-8-4.productionTip: Start with generous limits, observe metrics for a week, and only then tighten them.

l-9-1.title: GitOps Principles and Repository Structure
l-9-1.objectives: Understand GitOps principles | Structure repository by environment | Separate application from manifests
l-9-1.body: GitOps relies on four principles: desired state is declarative, versioned and immutable in Git, automatically applied by agents, with continuous reconciliation. The practical consequence is enormous: whoever can merge can deploy, and Git history is the history of what ran in production. | Separate the application repository from the manifest repository. The application generates a versioned image; the GitOps repository records which version should run in each environment. This allows for different review policies and prevents a code change from altering production without an explicit step. | Structure by environment with a common base and overlays: base/ with the essentials, overlays/dev and overlays/prod with replicas, resources, and host. Kustomize is ideal for this; Helm with per-environment values also works, and ArgoCD supports both.
l-9-1.whyItMatters: GitOps is the dominant standard for delivery in Kubernetes and increasingly appears in job descriptions.
l-9-1.commonMistake: Mixing code and manifests in the same repository and losing control over what goes to production.
l-9-1.productionTip: Protect the GitOps repository with mandatory review: it is the company's deploy button.

Installation is simple; the value lies in properly configuring the policy. | Auto-sync automatically applies changes. prune removes resources that are no longer in Git — powerful and dangerous, because a wrong path can delete objects. selfHeal undoes manual changes in the cluster, ensuring that Git prevails. In staging, turn on all three; in production, many teams maintain manual sync or with an approval window. | Use the interface and the CLI for diagnosis: health status per resource, diff between Git and cluster, sync history, and controller logs. It's the clearest view of 'what's running' an team can have.

Never 'resolve' OutOfSync by turning off self-heal. | Rollback in GitOps is a git revert of the commit that changed the image tag: the cluster returns to its previous state and the history records what happened. Promotion between environments is the same mechanism: a PR that updates the tag in the production overlay with the version already validated in staging.

mod-10.title: Observability and SRE
mod-10.tagline: Knowing what happens before the customer tells you.
mod-10.overview: Observability is not about installing Grafana: it's about being able to answer new questions about the system without a new deploy. You will instrument CloudShop with Prometheus metrics, centralize logs with Loki, distribute traces with OpenTelemetry, build dashboards that answer 'is everything okay?' in five seconds, define SLI/SLO with error budget, and conduct an incident to postmortem without blame.
mod-10.objectives: Differentiate logs, metrics, and traces and know when to use each | Write useful PromQL queries and actionable alert rules | Build RED and USE-guided dashboards | Define SLI, SLO, and error budget for CloudShop | Conduct an incident and write a postmortem without blame
mod-10.delivery: Dashboard, symptom-based alerts, documented SLO, incident runbook, and postmortem of a real event.
mod-10.checklist: Latency, error rate, and throughput metrics exposed by the API | Dashboard answers 'is everything okay?' without interpretation | Alerts based on user symptom, not CPU | SLO with calculated and documented error budget | Postmortem published with actions and owners
mod-10.troubleshooting: Symptom: users report slowness, CPU normal. Investigation: p95 latency metric increased, traces show 80% of time in a database query, database logs indicate a lock. Root cause: migration creating index on a large table during peak hours. Fix: abort migration, reschedule with concurrent creation, and alert based on p95, not CPU.
mod-10.interviewQuestions: Difference between SLI, SLO, and SLA? | What is error budget and how does it change product decisions? | How would you avoid alert fatigue in an on-call team?
mod-10.capstone: Instrument CloudShop with metrics, logs, traces, SLO, and useful alerts.
l-10-1.title: The three pillars and what to instrument first
l-10-1.objectives: Choose the appropriate signal for each question | Instrument the four essential metrics | Avoid explosive cardinality
l-10-1.body: Metrics answer 'how much and how often' cheaply and aggregated — ideal for alerting and trends. Logs answer 'what exactly happened in this event' — ideal for specific investigation. Traces answer 'where time was spent in this request that traversed five services'. Using the wrong signal costs time and money. | Start with the RED method for services: Rate (requests per second), Errors (error rate), and Duration (latency distribution). For resources, USE: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. With RED per route and USE per resource, you'll detect most real incidents. | Beware of cardinality: using userId, requestId, or full URL as a label multiplies time series and brings down Prometheus. Unique identifiers go into logs and traces; metric labels are low-cardinality dimensions (route, method, status).
l-10-1.whyItMatters: Uninstrumented service is a black box: you discover problems from the customer and debug by guessing.
l-10-1.commonMistake: Using full path with ID as a label and creating millions of series.
l-10-1.productionTip: Latency histogram with buckets aligned to your SLO; incorrect buckets render p95 useless.
l-10-1.securityAlert: Never put personal data in a metric label: it is retained for a long time and is difficult to expunge.
l-10-1.interviewQuestion: When would you use a trace instead of a log to investigate slowness?
l-10-1.glossaryDefs: Rate, Errors, Duration: a service-oriented monitoring method. | Number of distinct series generated by label combinations.
l-10-1.capstone: Expose /metrics in the CloudShop API with a latency histogram per route.
l-9-4.body: The GitOps paradox is clear: everything in Git, but secrets cannot go into Git in plain text. Two solutions dominate. External Secrets Operator keeps the value in a vault (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) and creates the Secret in the cluster from a versionable reference. SOPS encrypts the value in the file itself with a managed key (KMS), allowing for secure versioning. | External Secrets is usually the best choice when a corporate vault already exists: rotation happens in the vault, and the cluster follows. SOPS is excellent for small teams and for configuration that changes little, keeping the flow 100% in Git. | In any strategy, the same rules apply: periodic rotation, audited access, minimum scope, and no secrets in logs, ConfigMaps, or variables printed by pipelines.
l-9-4.whyItMatters: Leaked secrets in repositories are the most common and most preventable security incident in the industry.
l-9-4.commonMistake: Committing Secrets in base64 believing that base64 is encryption.
l-9-4.productionTip: Add a secret scanner to the CI of the GitOps repository; it prevents human error.
l-9-4.securityAlert: A committed secret is compromised forever: rotate, don't just remove the file.
l-9-4.interviewQuestion: How do you manage secrets in a GitOps flow?
l-9-4.glossaryDefs: Operator that synchronizes secrets from an external vault to cluster Secrets. | Tool that encrypts values inside YAML/JSON files using KMS or PGP.
l-9-4.capstone: Migrate the CloudShop database password to the vault with External Secrets.
l-9-4.codeLabels: External Secret referencing the vault | SOPS with KMS
l-9-4.codeNote0: The operator's ServiceAccount must only have permission on secrets with the cloudshop/ prefix.
l-9-4.q0: Base64 in a Kubernetes Secret offers:
l-9-4.q0opts: Strong encryption | Only encoding, no protection | Digital signature | Automatic rotation
l-9-4.q0exp: Base64 is reversible encoding; protection comes from RBAC, encryption at etcd, and vaults.
l-9-5.title: Image Pipeline + GitOps: the complete flow
l-9-5.objectives: Connect image CI to manifest updates | Automate version bumps via PR | Define deploy governance
l-9-5.body: The mature flow has two repositories and two roles. The application's CI tests, builds, and publishes the image with an immutable tag. Then, a step opens a PR in the GitOps repository, updating the environment's overlay tag. Whoever reviews this PR is authorizing the deploy. | For staging, this PR can be merged automatically — quick feedback is more valuable than ceremony. For production, human review and a defined window. This way, the same mechanism addresses two risk levels without different tools. | Alternative: ArgoCD Image Updater observes the registry and automatically updates the tag. It's convenient, but reduces the traceability of 'who decided to deploy'. For production, prefer the explicit PR.
l-9-5.whyItMatters: This is the delivery architecture that Platform Engineering job descriptions outline today.
l-9-5.commonMistake: Pushing directly to the GitOps repository's main branch via the pipeline, eliminating review.
l-9-5.productionTip: Record the build link, tests, and image digest in the PR: informed review in thirty seconds.
l-9-5.interviewQuestion: Describe the path of a commit to production in a GitOps architecture.
l-9-5.glossaryDefs: Component that automatically updates image tags from the registry. | Automated update of manifests after CI validation.
l-9-5.capstone: Automate CloudShop promotion to staging after green CI.
