l-10-1.codeNote0: Do not expose /metrics publicly: metrics reveal internal routes and business volumes. Restrict by network or authentication.
l-10-1.q0: Which label is inappropriate in a Prometheus metric?
l-10-1.q0exp: Unique identifiers generate practically infinite cardinality.
l-10-2.title: Prometheus and PromQL: queries and alerts worth being on-call for
l-10-2.objectives: Write PromQL for rate and percentile | Create alert rules by symptom | Configure routing in Alertmanager
l-10-2.body: Prometheus collects metrics by scraping and stores time series data. In PromQL, the rate function calculates the per-second rate of counters, histogram_quantile estimates percentiles from buckets, and aggregations by label allow observing behavior per route or per service. | A good alert is one that requires human action and describes the user impact: '5xx error rate above 2% for 5 minutes' is worth waking someone up for; 'CPU at 85%' usually isn't, because it can be healthy. Use 'for' to avoid alarms for transient spikes and set severity consistent with urgency. | In Alertmanager, group related alerts, define inhibition (don't alert on a symptom if the cause has already triggered), and routes by severity. Alert fatigue is an engineering failure: if the team ignores notifications, the alerting system is broken.
l-10-2.whyItMatters: Actionable alerts and linked runbooks are what make being on-call sustainable.
l-10-2.commonMistake: Alerting on CPU and disk but not alerting on user-perceived error rate.
l-10-2.productionTip: Every critical alert must have a link to a runbook with diagnostic and mitigation steps.
l-10-2.interviewQuestion: How would you define alerts for a new service without historical data?
l-10-2.glossaryDefs: PromQL function that calculates the per-second rate of a counter. | The speed at which the error budget is being consumed relative to what is allowed.
l-10-2.capstone: Create the CloudShop alert rules with a linked runbook.
l-10-2.codeLabels: Essential PromQL for CloudShop | Alert rules by symptom
l-10-2.codeNote1: Alert annotations go to chat channels: do not include customer data or sensitive log snippets.
l-10-2.q0opts: CPU above 80% | 5xx rate above 2% for 5 minutes | Disk at 60% | Number of pods greater than 3
l-10-2.q0exp: User-perceived error indicates real impact and requires action.
l-10-3.title: Grafana and Loki: centralized dashboards and logs
l-10-3.objectives: Build a dashboard that answers questions | Query logs with LogQL | Correlate metrics and logs
l-10-3.body: A dashboard is not a gallery of charts: it's a decision-making tool. The first panel answers 'is everything okay?' with error rate, p95, and throughput. The following ones help locate the problem: by route, by dependency, by resource. If a panel is never used during an incident, it just takes up space. | Loki indexes labels and stores compressed content, making it cheap and integrated with the same label model as Prometheus. With LogQL, you filter by stream and content, extract fields from JSON, and even generate metrics from logs. | The biggest gain is correlation: from the latency panel, go to the logs for that interval and service in two clicks. Standardizing structured logs with requestId and traceId is what allows closing the metric → log → trace cycle.
l-10-3.whyItMatters: During an incident, time spent looking for logs is downtime.
l-10-3.commonMistake: A dashboard with forty panels where nobody finds what matters.
l-10-3.productionTip: Place the SLO dashboard at the top and link the runbook in the dashboard description.
l-10-3.securityAlert: Centralized logs concentrate sensitive data: define retention and access control.
l-10-3.interviewQuestion: How do you correlate a latency spike with the corresponding logs?
l-10-3.glossaryDefs: Loki's query language, inspired by PromQL. | Log emitted as an object (JSON) with queryable fields.
l-10-3.capstone: Create the main CloudShop dashboard with SLO, RED, and a link to logs.
l-10-3.codeLabels: LogQL queries | Structured log in the application
l-10-3.codeNote1: Maintain a list of forbidden fields and an automated test that fails if any of them appear in the log.
l-10-3.q0: Which field is essential for correlating logs with traces?
l-10-3.q0opts: hostname | traceId | log level | timestamp only
l-10-3.q0exp: traceId links the log to the corresponding distributed request.
l-10-4.title: OpenTelemetry: Distributed Traces
l-10-4.objectives: Instrument traces with OTel | Understand context and propagation | Use sampling with criteria
l-10-4.body: A trace shows the journey of a request as a tree of spans, with duration and attributes for each step. It is the signal that immediately answers 'is the time spent in the database, in the external call, or in our code' — a question that aggregated metrics do not answer. | OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard: the SDK instruments the application, the Collector receives, processes, and exports to the chosen backend (Tempo, Jaeger, or managed service). Switching backends no longer means re-writing instrumentation. | Context propagation is what stitches services together: the traceparent travels in HTTP headers. And sampling controls cost — 100% in a study environment, a lower rate in production, always with a policy that preserves error traces and high-latency traces.
l-10-4.whyItMatters: In a distributed architecture, without traces, latency investigation is an educated guess.
l-10-4.commonMistake: Instrumenting only one service and losing propagation — the trace becomes broken.
l-10-4.productionTip: Tail sampling, preserving errors and slow requests, provides the best cost-benefit.
l-10-4.securityAlert: Never send the full request body to the trace backend.
l-10-4.interviewQuestion: What is context propagation and how does it work in HTTP?
l-10-4.glossaryDefs: A unit of work within a trace, with start, end, and attributes. | A process that receives, transforms, and exports telemetry to backends.
l-10-4.capstone: Trace the CloudShop order creation journey from frontend to database.
l-10-4.codeLabels: OTel instrumentation in the API | Collector with processing
l-10-4.codeNote0: Span attributes can leak sensitive data (request body, email). Configure redaction in the Collector.
l-10-4.q0: Which signal best indicates where a request's time was spent?
l-10-4.q0opts: Log | Aggregated metric | Distributed trace | Error counter
l-10-4.q0exp: Traces detail the duration of each step of the request.
l-10-5.title: SLI, SLO, Error Budget, and Blameless Postmortem
l-10-5.objectives: Define CloudShop SLI and SLO | Calculate and use error budget | Conduct incident and write postmortem
l-10-5.body: SLI is the measure of experience (e.g., proportion of successful requests under 500 ms). SLO is the internal goal for this indicator. SLA is the contractual commitment, usually looser than the SLO. Reliability stops being an opinion when there's a number. | Error budget is the complement of the SLO: with a goal of 99.9% over 30 days, you have about 43 minutes of allowed failure. This number guides decisions: a leftover budget allows accelerating deliveries; an exhausted budget requires prioritizing stability. It's the tool that ends the debate between 'delivering fast' and 'staying stable'. | Incidents have roles (commander, communication, investigation), a timeline log, and a focus on mitigating before understanding. Then comes the blameless postmortem: facts, measured impact, contributing causes, what worked, and actions with owner and deadline. Blaming people hides system failures and guarantees repetition.
l-10-5.whyItMatters: SLO and postmortem are SRE vocabulary for mid and senior-level interviews.
l-10-5.commonMistake: Defining a 99.99% SLO without the architecture or budget to sustain it.
l-10-5.productionTip: Alert by error budget burn rate, not by any deviation: drastically reduces noise.
l-10-5.securityAlert: Postmortem may contain sensitive customer data; publish an internal version and a sanitized version.
l-10-5.interviewQuestion: Explain error budget and how it influences the decision to launch a new feature.
l-10-5.glossaryDefs: Amount of failure allowed by the SLO within a time window. | Analysis focused on system and process failures, not on individuals.
l-10-5.capstone: Publish the CloudShop SLO and the module incident postmortem.
l-10-5.q0: A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows approximately how much downtime?
l-10-5.q0exp: 0.1% of 30 days is equivalent to about 43 minutes.
mod-11.title: DevSecOps, FinOps, and Final Project
mod-11.tagline: Secure, with controlled cost, and ready for portfolio.
mod-11.overview: The last module transforms what you've built into a project defensible in an interview. Security enters the pipeline (secrets, dependencies, images, supply chain), cost becomes an engineering metric, and documentation ties everything together: diagrams, recorded decisions, runbooks, and the narrative of each technical decision. This is where CloudShop stops being an exercise and becomes evidence of competence.
mod-11.objectives: Manage secrets with rotation and minimum scope | Add dependency, image, and IaC scans to the pipeline | Protect the supply chain with SBOM and signing | Optimize cost without violating the SLO | Document the project so another person can operate it
mod-11.delivery: Complete, secure, documented, and presentable CloudShop final project for interviews.
mod-11.checklist: No secrets in Git history (verified by scanner) | Pipeline fails on critical vulnerability with available fix | SBOM generated and image signed | Tested backup with proven restoration | README with architecture, decisions, cost, and runbooks
mod-11.troubleshooting: Symptom: scanner rejects the build due to a critical vulnerability in a transitive dependency with no fix. Correct decision: evaluate real exploitation in context (is the vulnerable function used?), apply mitigation, register an exception with a deadline and owner — do not disable the scanner. An exception without a deadline is a forgotten debt.
mod-11.interviewQuestions: How do you prevent a secret from reaching the repository? | What is SBOM and why have companies started requiring it? | How would you reduce the cost of an environment by 30% without affecting the SLO?
mod-11.capstone: Close CloudShop: security in the pipeline, documented cost, and portfolio presentation.
l-11-1.title: Secrets: lifecycle, rotation, and leak detection
l-11-1.objectives: Define where each secret lives | Automate rotation | Detect leaks in history
l-11-1.body: Every secret needs an answer to four questions: where it is stored, who can read it, how often it is rotated, and how we would know it leaked. Without these answers, you have passwords scattered in environment variables, screenshots, and chat messages. | The order of preference is clear: eliminate the secret (use federated identity like OIDC or instance role), then a managed vault with automatic rotation, and finally — if inevitable — a static secret with scheduled rotation and minimal scope. | Detection needs to be automatic: secret scanners in pre-commit and CI, including history scanning. And when a secret leaks, the procedure is to rotate immediately, audit usage, and only then clean the history. Removing the file does not undo the leak.
l-11-1.whyItMatters: Leaked credentials are the most frequent cause of compromise in cloud environments.
l-11-1.commonMistake: Deleting the file from the repository and considering the problem solved.
l-11-1.productionTip: Prefer federated identity: a secret that doesn't exist cannot leak.
l-11-1.securityAlert: Secrets in environment variables appear in error dumps and in misconfigured APM tools.
l-11-1.interviewQuestion: What is your procedure upon discovering a committed cloud key?
l-11-1.glossaryDefs: Periodic replacement of credentials, ideally automated. | Scanner that detects secret patterns in code and history.
l-11-1.capstone: Scan the history of CloudShop repositories and activate database secret rotation.
l-11-1.codeNote0: When finding a secret in history, consider it compromised: rotate before any cleanup.
l-11-1.q0: Upon finding a committed access key, the first action is to:
l-11-1.q0opts: Remove the file | Rotate/revoke the credential | Rewrite history | Make the repository private
l-11-1.q0exp: The credential is already exposed; revoking it stops misuse.
l-11-2.title: Scans, SBOM, and supply chain in the pipeline
l-11-2.objectives: Add scans to CI with clear policy | Generate SBOM | Sign and verify images
l-11-2.body: Security needs to be a pipeline stage, with explicit policy: fail on critical or high severity with available fix, warn on others, and log exceptions with a deadline. Without a policy, the scanner becomes noise that everyone ignores — or arbitrary blocking that everyone bypasses. | Cover all three layers: application dependencies (SCA), container image (operating system and libraries), and infrastructure as code (insecure configuration before provisioning). Finding a public bucket with tfsec takes seconds; discovering it in an audit costs reputation. | SBOM lists what exists in the artifact and is increasingly required in contracts; signing with cosign proves origin and integrity, allowing the cluster to accept only images signed by your pipeline.
l-11-2.whyItMatters: DevSecOps appears explicitly in job openings and is what allows fast delivery without becoming a risk.
l-11-2.commonMistake: Turning on all scanners without a policy and then turning them off because they 'block the team'.
l-11-2.productionTip: Require image signing in the cluster (policy controller): only run what your pipeline produced.
l-11-2.securityAlert: Typosquatting dependency installs malicious package during build. Pin versions and review lockfile in PR.
l-11-2.interviewQuestion: How would you define the vulnerability blocking policy in the pipeline?
l-11-2.glossaryDefs: Software Composition Analysis: analysis of dependencies and their vulnerabilities. | Sigstore project tool for signing and verifying artifacts.
l-11-2.capstone: Add scans and signing to the CloudShop pipeline.
l-11-2.codeNote0: ignore-unfixed prevents blocking due to vulnerabilities without a fix, but log them and review weekly.
l-11-2.q0opts: Accelerate the build | List artifact components for auditing and vulnerability response | Replace tests | Encrypt the image
l-11-2.q0exp: SBOM allows you to quickly know if you are affected by a new CVE.
l-11-3.title: FinOps: measure, attribute, and reduce cost
l-11-3.objectives: Attribute cost per project and environment | Apply right-sizing | Automate savings
l-11-3.body: FinOps starts with measuring and attributing: without consistent tags, cost is a single blob that no one can safely reduce. With attribution, you discover that 40% of spending is in a forgotten test environment — and saving becomes a trivial decision. | The most effective levers, in order: turn off what is not used, right-sizing based on real metrics, choose appropriate storage and class, use reserved or spot capacity for predictable/tolerant loads, and reduce inter-zone traffic. | Cost is an engineering decision with a reliability trade-off. Reducing replicas saves until you violate the SLO. This is why FinOps and SRE converse: the error budget is the limit of what savings can cost.
l-11-3.whyItMatters: Engineers who discuss cost with numbers participate in decisions — and that accelerates careers.
l-11-3.commonMistake: Cutting replicas and limits until violating the SLO, trading a smaller bill for an incident.
l-11-3.productionTip: Publish a cost dashboard per environment alongside the SLO dashboard: both conversations become honest.
l-11-3.interviewQuestion: How would you reduce cost by 30% while maintaining the SLO?
l-11-3.glossaryDefs: Adjusting resource size to observed actual consumption. | Deeply discounted capacity that can be interrupted by the provider.
l-11-3.capstone: Document CloudShop's monthly cost and apply two measured optimizations.
l-11-3.codeNote0: Automation that turns off resources needs scope by tag; without it, an error can bring down production.
l-11-3.q0: What is the prerequisite for attributing cost per environment?
l-11-3.q0opts: Configured budget | Consistent tags enabled for allocation | Reserved instances | Multi-AZ
l-11-3.q0exp: Without allocation tags, the report does not separate spending by environment or project.

lab-0-2.title: Cloud account secured with a budget

l-11-4.objectives: Write a README that supports a technical conversation | Record decisions with ADR | Prepare for the interview narrative
l-11-4.body: A project without documentation doesn't count as experience, because no one can evaluate it. The README needs to answer in two minutes: what it is, what the architecture is, how to run it, how to deploy it, how to observe it, how to revert it, how much it costs, and what decisions were made — with the why. | An ADR (Architecture Decision Record) is a short document per decision: context, options considered, choice, and consequences. It demonstrates exactly what a technical interview looks for: the ability to compare alternatives and make conscious trade-offs. | For the interview, prepare three two-minute stories: an incident you diagnosed (with evidence), an automation that reduced time or risk (with numbers), and an architectural decision with a trade-off. With CloudShop, you have real material for all three.
l-11-4.whyItMatters: In an interview, those who document can prove; those who don't document need to be believed.
l-11-4.commonMistake: README with only installation instructions, without architecture, decisions, or cost.
l-11-4.productionTip: Write the ADR at the time of the decision: reconstructing the reasoning later is never the same.
l-11-4.interviewQuestion: Tell me about an architectural decision you made, the alternatives, and the trade-off you accepted.
l-11-4.glossaryDefs: A short record of an architectural decision, with context and consequences. | Recovery Time Objective: target time to restore service.
l-11-4.capstone: Write the final README and the three main ADRs for CloudShop.
l-11-4.q0opts: Installation steps | Context, options, decision, and consequences of an architectural choice | Sprint task list | Service metrics
l-11-4.q0exp: It is the record of the reasoning and the trade-off made.
l-11-5.title: From completion to job offer: portfolio, resume, and interview
l-11-5.objectives: Transform the project into a portfolio | Write a results-oriented resume | Practice technical and behavioral interviews
l-11-5.body: A DevOps portfolio is not a list of technologies: it is evidence of operation. Organized repositories, a README with a diagram, a visible and green pipeline, dashboards with screenshots, a real postmortem, and ADRs. This is worth more than ten certificates without practice. | On your resume, each line should have a verb, scope, and measured result: 'reduced build time from 22 to 4 minutes with dependency caching and multi-stage' communicates competence; 'knowledge of Docker' communicates nothing. Numbers from your own project are legitimate and verifiable. | In an interview, the script is predictable: a Linux/network problem, a container/Kubernetes problem, a pipeline problem, a cloud/security problem, and a behavioral question about an incident. Rehearse out loud with CloudShop as a reference, always in three parts: situation, what you did, measured result.
l-11-5.whyItMatters: Competence without narrative doesn't lead to an offer. This lesson converts study into professional results.
l-11-5.commonMistake: Listing tools without ever having operated anything end-to-end.
l-11-5.productionTip: Record yourself answering the three stories: hearing your own answer corrects more than any tip.
l-11-5.interviewQuestion: Tell me about a project you built from scratch to production and what you would do differently today.
l-11-5.glossaryDefs: A set of verifiable evidence of what you know how to operate. | Response structure: situation, task, action, and result.
l-11-5.capstone: Publish CloudShop as the main project in your portfolio.
lab-1-1.title: 30 Linux Commands Runbook
lab-1-1.goal: Build an operational document with the 30 commands you will use in a real investigation.
lab-1-1.professionalContext: A runbook is what allows anyone on call to diagnose without depending on whoever wrote the system.
lab-1-1.steps: Group commands by objective: navigation, permissions, processes, logs, resources, network | For each command, write what it answers and when to use it | Test all commands on your machine | Add an 'incident first 5 minutes' section | Publish to docs/runbook-linux.md in the repository
lab-1-1.validation: 30 documented commands with purpose | Incident section with investigation order | Versioned file in Git
lab-1-1.errorNames: Commands copied without understanding | Runbook without usage order
lab-1-1.errorFixes: Explain each one with your own sentence; if you can't, you haven't learned yet | Order by diagnostic flow, not alphabetical order
lab-1-1.solution: A good runbook has an investigation order (load → memory → disk → processes → network → logs), tested commands, and an escalation criterion.
lab-1-2.title: systemd Service Resilient to Reboot and Failure
lab-1-2.goal: Put the CloudShop API under systemd with a dedicated user, automatic restart, and logs in the journal.
lab-1-2.professionalContext: Every service on a VM needs to start on boot and recover after failure, without human intervention.
lab-1-2.environment: Linux with systemd (WSL2 with systemd enabled or VM)
lab-1-2.steps: Create cloudshop system user without shell | Create /opt/cloudshop with correct owner and a minimal server.js | Write the unit with EnvironmentFile and Restart=on-failure | Enable, start, and validate with status and curl | Kill the process and confirm it restarts automatically
lab-1-2.commandsNote: app.env with 640 and service owner: environment variables should not be readable by any user.
lab-1-2.validation: systemctl is-enabled returns enabled | After killing the process, the service restarts in seconds | journalctl shows the application output
lab-1-2.errorFixes: Incorrect ExecStart path; use absolute path to the binary (which node) | Check journalctl for the actual error and increase RestartSec
lab-1-2.solution: With Restart=on-failure and enable, the service survives failure and reboot. The unit must use an unprivileged user and a protected EnvironmentFile.
lab-1-3.title: Hunting for Full Disk
lab-1-3.goal: Diagnose and resolve a /var at 100% without deleting necessary data.
lab-1-3.professionalContext: Full disk is one of the most frequent incidents and one that scares beginners the most.
lab-1-3.steps: Generate large files to simulate the problem | Detect saturation with df and locate the directory with du | Identify open and deleted files that still occupy space | Apply log rotation and secure cleanup | Configure preventive alert at 80%
lab-1-3.commandsNote: Never delete audit logs without a defined retention policy — it may be a legal requirement.
lab-1-3.validation: /var below 80% | Service continues writing logs normally | logrotate configured
lab-1-3.errorNames: Space not freed after rm | Disk free but out of space error
lab-1-3.errorFixes: The process keeps the handle open; use truncate or restart the service | Inodes exhausted; check df -i
lab-1-3.solution: df locates the partition, du the directory, lsof +L1 explains 'ghost' space. truncate resolves without breaking the process and logrotate prevents recurrence.
lab-2-1.title: Nginx reverse proxy with TLS for the API
lab-2-1.goal: Publish the API behind Nginx with HTTPS, correct headers, and defined timeouts.
lab-2-1.professionalContext: Standard configuration for any service exposed on the internet.
lab-2-1.environment: Linux with Nginx and certbot (or local self-signed certificate)
lab-2-1.steps: Install Nginx and create the CloudShop site | Configure upstream, proxy_set_header, and timeouts | Issue certificate (certbot or self-signed for laboratory) | Redirect HTTP to HTTPS | Validate headers and times with curl
lab-2-1.validation: HTTPS responds 200 on /health | HTTP redirects with 301 | X-Forwarded-For reaches the application
lab-2-1.errorFixes: Upstream is not listening; confirm with ss -tulpn and direct curl on 3000 | In distros with SELinux: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1
lab-2-1.solution: The proxy must forward Host and X-Forwarded-*, have short timeouts, and redirect HTTP. Errors in the error.log accurately indicate the cause of the 5xx.
lab-2-2.title: DNS and TTL Investigation
lab-2-2.goal: Diagnose why a DNS change 'did not propagate' and plan the migration correctly.
lab-2-2.professionalContext: Every infrastructure migration goes through DNS; an error here brings down the service for a portion of users.
lab-2-2.steps: Query the record on the local resolver and on a public one | Query the authoritative server and compare | Identify the TTL and calculate propagation time | Document a migration plan with prior TTL reduction | Validate the domain's TXT and NS records
lab-2-2.validation: You identify if the difference is cache or configuration | Documented TTL and written migration plan | Authoritative response compared with resolver's
lab-2-2.errorNames: Compare only the local resolver | Migrate with high TTL
lab-2-2.errorFixes: Always query the authoritative server to know the current truth | Reduce to 60s a few hours before and restore afterward
lab-2-2.solution: If the authoritative server already responds with the new IP and resolvers don't, it's cache: wait for the TTL. If the authoritative server responds with the old IP, the record was not saved.
lab-2-3.title: Measure latency per phase with curl
lab-2-3.goal: Separate DNS, connection, TLS, and processing to pinpoint where the slowness lies.
lab-2-3.professionalContext: Transforming 'it's slow' into a number per phase allows you to fix the right bottleneck.
lab-2-3.steps: Create an output format with times per phase | Measure 20 requests and calculate average and maximum | Compare access through proxy and directly to upstream | Record the result in the technical diary
lab-2-3.validation: You know which phase dominates the total time | Proxy versus upstream comparison recorded
lab-2-3.errorNames: A single measurement | Measure with browser cache
lab-2-3.errorFixes: Measure multiple times; isolated variation is misleading | Use curl, without cache and without extensions
lab-2-3.solution: High TLS suggests handshake/certificate; high TTFB suggests processing or database; high DNS suggests a bad resolver or too short a TTL.
lab-3-1.title: Merge conflict resolved safely
lab-3-1.goal: Create, diagnose, and resolve a real conflict, validating the result.
lab-3-1.professionalContext: Conflicts happen every week in a team; resolving them poorly introduces silent bugs.
lab-3-1.steps: Create two branches that modify the same line | Attempt rebase and observe the conflict | Resolve by choosing the correct result (not just one side) | Run tests and complete the rebase | Document the decision in the commit message body
lab-3-1.validation: No <<<<<<< markers remaining | Tests pass after resolution | Linear and readable history
lab-3-1.errorNames: Blindly accepting 'ours' or 'theirs' | Forgetting markers in the file
lab-3-1.errorFixes: Read both changes and decide the correct value | grep -rn '<<<<<<<' before committing
lab-3-1.solution: The correct resolution is sometimes a third value. After resolving, always run the tests: a poorly resolved conflict compiles and breaks in production.
lab-3-2.title: Health-check in Bash with retry and exit codes
lab-3-2.goal: Write a robust script that other processes can use to make decisions.
lab-3-2.professionalContext: Verification scripts feed cron, systemd, pipelines, and alerts.
lab-3-2.steps: Write the script with set -euo pipefail, trap, and log to stderr | Implement 3 retries with backoff | Return distinct codes per failure type | Pass shellcheck without warnings | Test against a valid and an invalid URL
lab-3-2.validation: exit 0 on happy path | exit 3 when the service doesn't respond | shellcheck without warnings
lab-3-2.errorNames: Script returns 0 even on failure | Unquoted variable breaking with spaces
lab-3-2.errorFixes: Ensure explicit exit on each path | Always use "$var"
lab-3-2.solution: Distinct exit codes allow automation to differentiate 'missing dependency' from 'service down', which changes the action taken.
lab-3-3.title: Log backup with retention and tested restoration
lab-3-3.goal: Automate daily backup and prove that restoration works.
lab-3-3.professionalContext: Untested backup is not backup — it's hope.
lab-3-3.steps: Write the backup script with integrity validation | Apply 14-day retention | Create systemd service and timer | Perform restoration in a temporary directory | Document the procedure in the runbook
lab-3-3.commandsNote: Backup directory with 700 permissions: logs might contain personal data.
lab-3-3.validation: Valid .tar.gz file generated | Restoration recovers files | Files older than 14 days removed
lab-3-3.errorNames: tar fails due to absolute path | Timer doesn't trigger
lab-4-3.goal: Run the application without privileges, with a read-only filesystem, and limited resources.
lab-4-3.professionalContext: A requirement for any security checklist in a corporate environment.
lab-4-3.steps: Create user in Dockerfile and adjust file ownership | Run with --read-only and tmpfs on paths that need to write | Drop capabilities and prevent privilege escalation | Define memory and CPU limits | Confirm behavior with tests
lab-4-3.commandsNote: If the application needs to write, mount tmpfs only on necessary paths — never remove the entire read-only setting.
lab-4-3.validation: id shows non-root user | Filesystem write fails | Limits appear in docker inspect
lab-4-3.errorNames: Application fails because it cannot write cache | EACCES when reading image files
lab-4-3.errorFixes: Mount tmpfs in the specific directory | COPY --chown to the application user
lab-4-3.solution: Non-root + read-only + cap-drop ALL + limits is the baseline configuration. Each exception must be justified and minimal.
lab-5-1.title: Complete CI in PR: lint, tests, and build

lab-5-1.professionalContext: Minimum standard for any team delivering multiple times a week.

lab-5-1.validation: PR with error is blocked | Pipeline under 5 minutes | Cache reduces time on second run
lab-5-1.errorNames: Cache is never reused | Check does not appear in protection
lab-5-1.errorFixes: Key based on lockfile hash | The workflow needs to run once for the context to exist
lab-5-1.solution: Mandatory green for merge is what gives the team confidence. Measure duration and treat slowness as a bug.
lab-5-2.title: Publish image to GHCR with immutable tag
lab-5-2.goal: Generate a versioned image with metadata and record the digest.
lab-5-2.professionalContext: Traceability between commit, image, and what's running in production.
lab-3-3.errorFixes: Use tar -C directory . for relative paths | Check OnCalendar and Persistent, and use systemctl list-timers

lab-4-1.title: Full CloudShop Stack with Docker Compose

lab-4-1.professionalContext: A reproducible development environment is standard delivery for platform owners.

lab-4-1.errorNames: ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432 | API restarts before the database comes up
lab-4-1.errorFixes: Use DATABASE_HOST=db; localhost is the container itself | healthcheck on db + condition: service_healthy
lab-4-1.solution: With healthcheck and conditional depends_on, the startup order is no longer luck. Named volume ensures persistence between recreations.
lab-4-2.title: Reduce image from 1.2 GB to less than 200 MB
lab-4-2.goal: Apply multi-stage, slim base, and .dockerignore, measuring the result.
lab-4-2.professionalContext: Smaller image reduces pipeline time, registry cost, and attack surface.

lab-4-2.validation: Final image below 200 MB | Application continues to respond | No critical vulnerabilities with available fixes
lab-4-2.errorNames: npm ci fails in the runtime stage | Native binary breaks on Alpine
lab-4-2.errorFixes: Copy node_modules from the deps stage instead of reinstalling | Use the slim variant of Debian or compile in the same environment

lab-4-3.title: Harden the container: non-root, read-only, and limits
lab-5-2.steps: Add login, metadata, and build-push to the workflow | Create the v0.1.0 tag and trigger the workflow | Check published tags in the package | Register the digest in the release file | Pull the image locally by digest and run

lab-5-2.errorNames: denied: permission_denied on push | latest tag overwritten in production
lab-5-2.errorFixes: Add packages: write to job permissions | Never use latest for deploy; always use version or digest

lab-5-3.title: Automatic rollback on health failure
lab-5-3.goal: Make the pipeline automatically revert when the deployment is unhealthy.
lab-5-3.professionalContext: Reduces restoration time from tens of minutes to just a few.
lab-5-3.steps: Record the current version before applying the new one | Apply the new version and run health check | Automatically revert in case of failure | Intentionally provoke a failure and measure restoration time | Document the measured RTO in the README
lab-5-3.validation: Bad deploy is automatically reverted | Service responds 200 again | Restoration time recorded
lab-5-3.errorNames: Rollback does not run | Health-check passes too early
lab-5-3.errorFixes: Add if: failure() to the revert step | Wait for readiness and repeat the check with backoff
lab-5-3.solution: Post-deploy verification with automatic rollback is the cheapest mechanism to protect production. Measure and publish the RTO.
lab-6-1.title: CloudShop VPC with public and private subnets
lab-6-1.goal: Build the complete network and prove that the private subnet is not reachable from outside.
lab-6-1.professionalContext: The foundation of any auditable cloud environment.

lab-6-1.commandsNote: Confirm in the console that nothing is left: NAT and Elastic IP continue to incur charges after the lab.
lab-6-1.validation: Private instance without public IP | Route to IGW only in the public route table | Account with no remaining resources
lab-6-1.errorNames: DependencyViolation when deleting the VPC | Bill with forgotten NAT
lab-6-1.errorFixes: Remove in order: instances, NAT, ENIs, subnets, IGW, VPC | Check describe-nat-gateways and addresses at the end of every lab

lab-6-2.title: Frontend on S3 with CloudFront and private bucket
lab-6-2.goal: Publish the site with HTTPS and CDN without making the bucket public.
lab-6-2.professionalContext: Standard and most economical architecture for SPA in production.
lab-6-2.steps: Create private bucket with encryption and public access block | Publish the Vue build | Create CloudFront distribution with OAC | Adjust cache and error page for SPA | Validate HTTPS and cache invalidation
lab-6-2.validation: Direct access to the bucket returns 403 | CloudFront serves the site with HTTPS | SPA route works after refresh

lab-6-2.errorFixes: Bucket policy must allow the distribution's OAC | Configure 404 error response to /index.html with status 200

lab-6-3.title: Private RDS with managed secret and tested backup
lab-6-3.goal: Spin up a managed PostgreSQL without public access and restore a backup.
lab-6-3.professionalContext: Database is the most critical resource; an untried backup is the most expensive mistake.
lab-6-3.steps: Create subnet group with private subnets | Create instance with managed password and no public access | Connect via bastion/tunnel and create test data | Restore a snapshot to a new instance and validate the data | Destroy both instances
lab-6-3.commandsNote: Never print the database password to the terminal or in pipeline logs.
lab-6-3.validation: PubliclyAccessible = false | Backup with retention greater than zero | Data present in the restored instance
lab-6-3.errorNames: Timeout when connecting | Restoration without expected data
lab-6-3.errorFixes: RDS SG must allow the correct source; use SG reference | Snapshot created before writing; check the time
lab-6-3.solution: Private database, password in vault, backup with retention, and proven restoration. Only then can the environment be called ready.
lab-7-1.title: Terraform with remote state and two environments

lab-7-1.professionalContext: How real teams manage multiple environments without duplicating code.

lab-7-1.validation: State in S3, not local | plan returns exit 0 after apply | Module reused by both environments
lab-7-1.errorNames: Error acquiring the state lock | Duplicate resources between environments
lab-7-1.errorFixes: Another execution in progress; wait or force-unlock carefully | Names derived from var.env in all resources

lab-7-2.title: Provoke and resolve Terraform drift
lab-7-2.goal: Change a resource via the console, detect the divergence, and reconcile.
lab-7-2.professionalContext: Drift happens in every company after emergency console fixes.
lab-7-2.steps: Apply the infrastructure and confirm a clean plan | Manually change a tag or SG rule via CLI | Detect divergence with plan -detailed-exitcode | Decide: reflect in code or revert to desired state | Configure the scheduled drift detection job

lab-7-2.errorFixes: Reflect the fix in the code first; then apply | Use lifecycle ignore_changes for the specific attribute

lab-7-3.title: Idempotent Ansible playbook for the API host
lab-7-3.goal: Configure the entire host using a playbook, proving idempotence.

lab-8-1.title: CloudShop on Kubernetes (Kind) end-to-end

lab-8-2.title: Probes and limits against false incidents
lab-8-2.goal: Configure correct probes and observe OOMKilled in practice.
lab-8-2.professionalContext: Poorly configured probes and limits cause recurring instability in real clusters.

lab-8-3.title: Helm Chart with proven rollback

lab-9-1.title: ArgoCD syncing CloudShop

lab-9-2.title: Production rollback by git revert

lab-9-3.title: Secrets outside Git with External Secrets

lab-10-1.title: CloudShop observability stack and dashboard

lab-10-2.title: Actionable alerts with linked runbook
lab-10-2.goal: Create alerts by user symptom and test the actual trigger.
lab-10-2.professionalContext: Bad alerts cause fatigue; good alerts prevent prolonged downtime.
lab-10-2.steps: Write error rate, p95, and burn rate rules | Link runbook in annotations | Configure route by severity in Alertmanager | Provoke errors in the API and observe the trigger | Adjust 'for' until false positives are eliminated

lab-10-3.title: Distributed Traces with OpenTelemetry

lab-10-4.title: SLO, error budget, and postmortem

lab-10-4.validation: SLO documented with query and budget | Impact measured in minutes and budget | Postmortem published with actions
lab-10-4.errorNames: SLO without associated query | Postmortem blaming a person
lab-10-4.errorFixes: Every SLO needs a measurable expression | Describe system failures, process failures, and lack of guardrails

lab-11-1.title: Secret scanning in Git history

lab-11-2.title: Security pipeline with blocking policy
lab-11-2.goal: Block the build on critical, remediable vulnerabilities and register exceptions with deadlines.

lab-11-3.title: Cost optimization with a target and without violating the SLO
lab-11-3.goal: Reduce the environment cost and prove that the SLO remained intact.
lab-11-3.professionalContext: FinOps in practice: savings justified by data, not by blind cuts.
lab-11-3.steps: Estimate cost per service and per environment | Choose three measurable optimizations | Apply and measure the effect on cost | Compare SLI before and after | Record the result in the README
lab-11-3.commandsNote: Automated shutdown must filter by tag env=dev; without a filter, the risk is bringing down production.
lab-11-3.validation: Cost reduction measured in percentage | SLI maintained within target | Documented optimizations
lab-11-3.errorNames: Savings with availability drop | Cost without attribution
lab-11-3.errorFixes: Revert and choose another lever; SLO is the limit | Enable cost allocation tags before measuring
lab-11-3.solution: Good optimization has a number before, a number after, and an intact SLO. This trio is what you present in an interview.
lab-11-4.title: Final portfolio: README, ADRs, and diagram
lab-11-4.goal: Get CloudShop ready to be evaluated by a technical recruiter.
lab-11-4.professionalContext: It's the artifact that converts study into an interview.
lab-11-4.steps: Write the README with architecture, deployment, observability, rollback, and cost | Create three ADRs for the main decisions | Generate the architecture diagram | Add CI badges and dashboard screenshots | Ask someone else for a review and adjust what wasn't clear
lab-11-4.validation: Another person can run the project using the README | Three ADRs published | Diagram rendering on GitHub
lab-11-4.errorNames: README with only installation commands | Diagram without delivery flow
lab-11-4.errorFixes: Include architecture, decisions, cost, and rollback | Also show CI, registry, and GitOps
lab-11-4.solution: The portfolio needs to answer what it is, how it operates, how it fails, how it recovers, and how much it costs. This is what differentiates a project from a tutorial.
ch-01.title: On-call runbook in 30 commands
ch-01.brief: Write the runbook that anyone would use in the first five minutes of an incident on a Linux server, including investigation order and escalation criteria.
ch-01.acceptance: 30 commands grouped by objective, each with its own phrase explaining what it answers | 'First 5 minutes' section with justified execution order | Objective escalation criteria (when to involve another person) | Versioned file in docs/runbook-linux.md
ch-01.feedback: Simulated evaluation: runbooks fail when they list commands without usage order. The differentiator is telling what to do with each result.
ch-02.title: Diagnosing 502 without touching the code
ch-02.brief: Given an Nginx returning intermittent 502, produce a report with evidence that proves the root cause without changing the application.
ch-02.acceptance: Evidence from Nginx's error.log with the message in parentheses | Direct test on the upstream with curl and port verification with ss | Temporal correlation between service restarts and 502 occurrences | Conclusion with root cause and proposed fix (with and without code change)
ch-02.feedback: Strong reports distinguish 502 from 504 by evidence, not assumption, and propose a structural fix beyond palliative measures.
ch-03.title: On-call automation in Bash
ch-03.brief: Deliver two scripts (health-check and backup with retention) with error handling, distinct exit codes, and scheduling by systemd timer.
ch-03.acceptance: set -euo pipefail, cleanup trap and log with timestamp to stderr | Different exit codes per failure type, documented in the header | ShellCheck without warnings | Active timer with Persistent=true and tested backup restoration
ch-03.feedback: What fails here is a script that returns 0 on failure: downstream automation makes wrong decisions and the problem passes silently.
ch-04.title: Lean and hardened image
ch-04.brief: Reduce the API image to less than 200 MB, running as a non-root user, with a read-only filesystem and no critical corrigible vulnerabilities.
ch-04.acceptance: Size before and after documented, with the three changes that produced the gain | Multi-stage with .dockerignore and production dependencies only | Container runs with --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, and non-root user | Trivy without fixable HIGH/CRITICAL
ch-04.feedback: Good candidates explain the gain per layer; mediocre ones just switch the base to alpine and stop there.
ch-05.title: Complete stack with one command
ch-05.brief: Deliver a docker compose up that brings up frontend, API, and database with healthchecks, persistence, and no secrets in plain text in the repository.
ch-05.acceptance: Healthcheck on the database and depends_on with condition: service_healthy | Named volume with proven persistence after down/up | Internal network for the database, without published port on the host | Secrets via file or secret, with corresponding .gitignore
ch-05.feedback: Reviewers test exactly two things: bringing up from scratch on a clean machine and surviving a restart without data loss.
ch-06.title: Pipeline that protects main
ch-06.brief: Configure mandatory CI with lint, unit and integration tests, efficient cache, and total duration below five minutes.
ch-06.acceptance: Merge blocked when check fails | Integration tests with service container and applied migrations | Cache with key based on lockfile, with measured gain | Pipeline duration documented before and after optimizations
ch-06.feedback: Slow pipeline is the most common problem: show the number before and after and explain what caused the gain.
ch-07.title: Deploy with automatic rollback
ch-07.brief: Implement image publication with immutable tag and deploy that automatically rolls back when the health check fails. Measure RTO.
ch-07.acceptance: Image published with semantic version, SHA tag and registered digest | Post-deploy health check with retry and backoff | Automatic rollback on failure, with execution evidence | RTO measured and published in README
ch-07.feedback: Whoever measures RTO stands out. An existing but never-tested rollback is considered non-existent by good evaluators.
ch-08.title: Secure and Auditable AWS Environment
ch-08.brief: Deliver an environment with a private database, application in a private subnet, IAM without static keys, configured budget, and executed destruction checklist.
ch-08.acceptance: No long-term access keys in use (OIDC or instance profile) | Audit showing zero 0.0.0.0/0 rules on administrative or database ports | Active budget and all resources with project/environment/owner tags | Evidence that the account had no remaining resources at the end
ch-08.feedback: The finding that most frequently fails real audits is SSH or database port open to the world — verify before delivering.
ch-09.title: Two Identical Environments via IaC
ch-09.brief: Provision dev and staging with the same module, remote state with lock, and configure hosts with an idempotent playbook.
ch-09.acceptance: State in remote backend with versioning, lock, and encryption | Reused module; differences only in tfvars | terraform plan with exit code 0 after apply in both environments | Playbook with changed=0 on the second execution
ch-09.feedback: Those who duplicate code per environment fail. The goal is one definition, multiple configurations.
ch-10.title: Kubernetes with Proven Rollback
ch-10.brief: Run CloudShop on the cluster with Ingress, correct probes, limits sized by measurement, and rollback executed with recorded time.
ch-10.acceptance: Probes separating liveness (no dependencies) from readiness (with dependencies) | requests/limits justified by kubectl top, not by guesswork | Helm Chart with values per environment and mandatory image.tag | Evidence of rollback with measured time
ch-10.feedback: Liveness that checks the database is the classic mistake: explain why you didn't do that and earn points.
ch-11.title: End-to-End GitOps
ch-11.brief: Put staging and production under ArgoCD, with promotion via PR, secrets outside Git, and rollback by proven revert.
ch-11.acceptance: Applications Synced/Healthy with selfHeal active in staging | Promotion to production via PR with the version validated in staging | No sensitive values in the GitOps repository (verified by scanner) | Rollback via git revert with recorded time
ch-11.feedback: Senior-level differentiator: explain why production doesn't have auto-sync and how self-heal interacts with HPA.
ch-12.title: SLO, Incident, and Postmortem
ch-12.brief: Define CloudShop SLOs, conduct a controlled incident, and publish a blameless postmortem with actions, owners, and deadlines.
ch-12.acceptance: Two SLIs with PromQL query and justified targets | Alerts by symptom and by burn rate, with linked runbook | Incident timeline with measured impact in minutes and error budget | Postmortem with contributing causes, what worked, and actions with deadlines
ch-12.feedback: A postmortem that blames a person is rejected. What is evaluated is the ability to find the system failure that allowed the error.
boss-processo-zumbi.name: Zombie Process
boss-processo-zumbi.scenario: After a manual deploy, the API service fails to start: port 3000 is occupied, systemd reports failure, and there are orphaned processes in the tree. The team requests the API back online in ten minutes.
boss-processo-zumbi.symptoms: systemctl start fails with 'Address already in use' | ps shows node processes in Z (zombie) state and an old parent still alive | journalctl records successive restarts
boss-out-of-sync.resolution: Remove replicas from the versioned manifest (or use ignoreDifferences in /spec/replicas) | Leave HPA as the sole authority over replica count, with a safe minReplicas | Synchronize and confirm Synced/Healthy with HPA operating | Document in the repository who owns each field | Prevention: review every field mutated by controllers before versioning it
boss-queda-producao.name: Production Outage
boss-queda-producao.scenario: 2:03 PM. Critical alert: 78% of requests failing after v1.4.0 deployment. You are the incident commander. Every minute consumes error budget from a 99.9% SLO.
boss-queda-producao.symptoms: 5xx rate above 70%, p95 above 8 seconds | Traces show long wait times before database queries | Database logs indicate connection limit reached
boss-queda-producao.investigationSteps: Confirm impact and scope on the dashboard | Check what changed in the last 30 minutes | Locate the bottleneck in the trace | Confirm the hypothesis in the database logs | After mitigation, validate recovery
boss-queda-producao.rootCause: v1.4.0 opened a connection per request without returning it to the pool. Under normal traffic, the database connection limit was reached in two minutes, causing widespread failure. The load test did not cover the new route.
boss-queda-producao.resolution: Mitigate first: rollback via git revert and sync (service restored before complete analysis) | Communicate status every 10 minutes, with impact and next update | Confirm recovery by metrics, not by feeling | Fix the connection leak and cover with a test that fails without the fix | Add a pool saturation alert and write a blameless postmortem with actions, owners, and deadlines

boss-pipeline-quebrado.rootCause: The main job used an environment secret that only exists in the PR environment; after a credential rotation, the variable diverged between the two paths. Configuration duplication between workflows hid the problem.
boss-pipeline-quebrado.resolution: Unify common steps into a reusable workflow (workflow_call) with the same variables | Use ephemeral test credentials from the service container, never a real secret in test | Add validation that fails early when a mandatory variable is missing | Rerun only failed jobs to confirm the fix | Prevention: prohibit configuration duplication between workflows and review secret rotation as a change
boss-security-group.name: Exposed Security Group
boss-security-group.scenario: A security scan found the database's port 5432 accessible from 0.0.0.0/0 and SSH open to the world. You have one hour to fix it without bringing down the application.
boss-security-group.symptoms: 0.0.0.0/0 rule on port 5432 of the DB SG | 0.0.0.0/0 rule on port 22 of the application SG | CloudTrail logs authentication attempts from unknown IPs
boss-security-group.investigationSteps: List SGs with rules open to the world | Confirm if the database is publicly accessible | Find out who really needs access | Audit access attempts | Validate the new rule before removing the old one
boss-security-group.rootCause: Rules manually created 'for testing' during initial provisioning, without IaC and without review. The database became reachable from the internet and SSH exposed to brute force.
boss-security-group.resolution: Add the correct rule (5432 with source from the application SG) before removing the open one, avoiding unavailability | Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 rules from 22 and 5432 and replace SSH with SSM Session Manager | Confirm PubliclyAccessible=false on RDS and rotate database credentials | Describe SGs in Terraform so the change is versioned and reviewable | Prevention: automated verification in CI that fails on rules open to the world
boss-drift-terraform.name: Terraform Drift
boss-drift-terraform.scenario: The routine plan wants to destroy a firewall rule and change tags that no one changed in the code. There was an emergency fix in the console the previous dawn.
boss-drift-terraform.symptoms: terraform plan returns exit code 2 with unexpected changes | A manually created rule resolved an incident and is not in the code | Resource tags diverge from the project standard
boss-drift-terraform.investigationSteps: See exactly what differs | Compare the state with reality | Find out who changed and when | Reflect the legitimate change in the code | Confirm convergence after adjustment
boss-drift-terraform.rootCause: Manual change in the console during an incident (drift). The subsequent apply would remove a legitimate fix, turning the IaC routine into a new incident.
boss-drift-terraform.resolution: DO NOT apply before understanding: identify which differences are legitimate and which are accidental | Bring the legitimate fix to the code (or import the manually created resource) | Revert accidental differences by applying the code | Confirm plan with exit code 0 in both environments | Prevention: daily scheduled plan in CI, drift alert, and rule that manual fixes become PRs on the same day
boss-crashloopbackoff.name: CrashLoopBackOff
boss-crashloopbackoff.scenario: After an upgrade, two API pods enter CrashLoopBackOff with 14 restarts. The previous version was working, and the cluster has available resources.
boss-crashloopbackoff.symptoms: kubectl get pods shows CrashLoopBackOff and increasing restart count | describe indicates Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled in one pod and liveness failure in the other | Container logs end during initialization
boss-crashloopbackoff.investigationSteps: Check state and restarts | Read events and termination reason | Read previous execution logs | Confirm OOMKilled | Measure actual consumption of the healthy version
boss-crashloopbackoff.rootCause: The new version increased memory consumption at startup and exceeded the 256Mi limit (OOMKilled). In parallel, the liveness probe with a short initialDelay killed the container before it finished initializing, creating the loop.
boss-crashloopbackoff.resolution: Mitigate with immediate rollback: kubectl rollout undo (or helm rollback) to restore the service | Size requests/limits based on the measured consumption of the new version | Add a startupProbe with a generous failureThreshold and keep the liveness simple, without dependencies | Reapply the version with adjustments and observe rollout status | Prevention: load testing in CI comparing consumption between versions and OOMKilled alert
boss-out-of-sync.name: Deployment Out Of Sync
boss-out-of-sync.scenario: The production Application has been OutOfSync for hours and self-heal keeps undoing the number of replicas adjusted by autoscaling, fluctuating capacity during peak hours.
boss-out-of-sync.symptoms: ArgoCD reports OutOfSync in the spec.replicas field | Replicas fluctuate between the Git value and the HPA value | Latency increases during fluctuations
boss-out-of-sync.investigationSteps: Check status and last synchronization | Find out exactly which field differs | Confirm that HPA is active | Check sync history | Verify if someone manually edited the cluster
boss-out-of-sync.rootCause: Conflict between two sources of truth for the same field: Git declares replicas and HPA also manages them. Self-heal reverted autoscaling, and HPA scaled again — a tug-of-war in production.

boss-processo-zumbi.investigationSteps: View the unit status and the exact error | Discover who occupies the port | Map the process tree and zombies | Read the unit's first error | Confirm open files and sockets
boss-processo-zumbi.rootCause: A previous manual execution left a node process running in the background, holding port 3000. Its children terminated without being reaped (zombies), and systemd couldn't start the unit because the socket was already in use.
boss-processo-zumbi.resolution: Terminate the orphaned parent process with SIGTERM (kill -TERM) to allow cleanup | Confirm that the zombies disappeared along with the parent | Verify that the port is free with ss -tulpn | Start the unit via systemd and confirm 200 on /health | Prevention: prohibit manual execution of the binary and always use systemctl; add KillMode=control-group to the unit
boss-dragao-502.name: 502 Dragon
boss-dragao-502.scenario: Users receive 502s in two-minute bursts, several times an hour. The application team guarantees that 'nothing changed'. You have access to the proxy and the API host.
boss-dragao-502.symptoms: Nginx returns intermittent 502; between bursts, everything is normal | error.log shows 'connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream' | Host memory usage grows until the time of the bursts
boss-dragao-502.investigationSteps: Read the exact proxy message | Test the upstream directly | Confirm who is listening on the port | Check for restarts and OOM in the unit | Correlate 502 times with restarts
boss-dragao-502.rootCause: The API was terminated by the OOM killer due to a memory leak and restarted by systemd. During the seconds of restart, Nginx could not connect to the upstream and returned 502s — hence the burst pattern.
boss-dragao-502.resolution: Mitigate immediately: increase available memory and reduce downtime window with readiness before receiving traffic | Configure max_fails/fail_timeout and retry in Nginx upstream | Fix the leak (evidence: growing heap between restarts) | Add alert for 5xx rate and for unit restarts | Document in the runbook: 502 = unavailable upstream; 504 = slow upstream
boss-conflito-merge.name: Merge Conflict
boss-conflito-merge.scenario: An urgent fix needs to go into main, but your branch is three days behind and conflicts in two files, including a timeout configuration file that someone else also changed.
boss-conflito-merge.symptoms: git rebase stops with CONFLICT in two files | The branch has commits already pushed and reviewed in the PR | One of the conflicts is semantic: both values are plausible
boss-conflito-merge.investigationSteps: See which files conflict | Understand what each side changed | See the diff of the conflicting file | Find out who changed the value and why | After resolving, validate with tests
boss-conflito-merge.rootCause: Long divergence between branch and main plus simultaneous change to the same parameter. The textual conflict hides an engineering decision: which timeout is correct.
boss-conflito-merge.resolution: Resolve the conflict by choosing the correct value (which might not be either of the two) and record why in the commit | Run tests before concluding the rebase | Conclude with git rebase --continue and push with --force-with-lease (never --force) | If the PR already had approvals, notify reviewers of the rewrite | Prevention: short branches, daily integration with main, and tests covering the altered parameter
boss-crashloop-container.name: Container CrashLoop
boss-crashloop-container.scenario: After adding the database to Compose, the API enters a restart loop. The frontend responds, but no data-dependent routes work.
boss-crashloop-container.symptoms: docker compose ps shows api continuously restarting | Logs always end with ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432 | The database is healthy
boss-crashloop-container.investigationSt: See the actual application error | Confirm database health | Test name resolution inside the container | Inspect effective variables | Check the entrypoint and command
boss-crashloop-container.rootCause: The application connected to 127.0.0.1, which inside the container is the container itself, not the database service. In addition, there was no healthcheck with conditional depends_on, so the API started before the database could accept connections.
boss-crashloop-container.resolution: Define DATABASE_HOST=db (service name in Compose) | Add healthcheck with pg_isready to the database and condition: service_healthy to the API | Implement retry with backoff for the application's initial connection | Put the database in an internal network, without a published port | Prevention: validate with docker compose config in CI and test startup from a clean machine
boss-pipeline-quebrado.name: Broken Pipeline
boss-pipeline-quebrado.scenario: CI has been green on PRs and red on main since last night. No one changed the workflow, and the team is blocked from releasing the version.
boss-pipeline-quebrado.symptoms: Integration job fails only on main, at the migration step | Log shows 'password authentication failed for user' | Locally everything passes
boss-pipeline-quebrado.investigationStep: See the first error of the failed job | Compare green and red executions | Check for variable differences between triggers | Reproduce locally with the same versions | Confirm the service container and the connection string
